591.q: If {{name}} has data on smoking and lung disease, can they decide whether the two are independent?

584.desc: Find the critical region for a test (the values of the test statistic that lead to rejecting H₀) and decide the outcome by checking whether the observed value lies in it
584.ev: Finds a critical region for a one-tailed binomial test
584.q: If {{name}} tests H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3 with 20 trials at 5%, can they find the critical region?

595.desc: Find P(X ≤ r), P(X ≥ r) and probabilities of ranges for a Poisson variable using cumulative functions, taking care with inequalities for a discrete variable
595.q: If {{name}} needs the probability of at least 3 breakdowns in a month for X ~ Po(1.8), can they find it from cumulative probabilities?

594.desc: Find P(X ≤ r), P(X ≥ r) and P(a ≤ X ≤ b) for a binomial distribution using cumulative functions, taking care with inequalities on a discrete variable
594.q: If {{name}} needs the probability of at least 4 successes in 12 trials, can they rewrite it using P(X ≤ 3)?

596.desc: Use sample survey data to estimate a population mean or proportion, and develop a margin of error through simulation
596.ev: Estimates a population proportion from a sample
596.q: If {{name}} reads that 52% of voters support a candidate ± 3%, can they explain what the ± 3% means?

597.desc: Evaluate reports and news stories that use data, checking study type, sample, measures used, graphs and whether conclusions are justified
597.ev: Identifies the study type behind a headline
597.q: If {{name}} reads a headline that 'video games make children violent', can they ask the right questions about the data behind it?

599.desc: Calculate the expected value of a random variable as the probability-weighted mean, and interpret it as a long-run average
599.ev: Calculates expected value from a distribution
599.q: If {{name}} plays a game paying £5 with probability 0.1 and costing £1 to play, can they work out the expected gain?

600.desc: Use two-way tables or tree diagrams to find the probability that a positive test result is correct, explaining why rare conditions give many false positives
600.ev: Builds a table for a test with given accuracy
600.q: If {{name}} is told a test is 95% accurate for a condition 1 in 1000 people have, can they explain why most positives are false?

601.desc: Fit quadratic and exponential functions to data with technology, compare them with a linear fit using residuals, and choose the most appropriate model
601.ev: Fits an exponential model to population data
601.q: If {{name}} has data on a cooling cup of tea, can they decide whether a linear or exponential model fits better?

604.desc: Carry out a complete hypothesis test for a binomial proportion: hypotheses, null distribution, p-value or critical region, decision and conclusion in context
604.q: If {{name}} hears that 7 out of 10 people preferred a new cola when 50% was expected, can they carry out a test at 5% and state a conclusion?

605.desc: Critique a binomial model in context, identifying where independence or constant probability may fail (e.g. seeds in the same tray, free throws when tired), and describe the effect on conclusions
605.ev: Identifies an assumption that may fail
605.q: If {{name}} models a basketball player's 20 free throws as binomial, can they explain why the model might not be realistic?

607.desc: Use E(X) = Var(X) = λ for a Poisson distribution, and compare a sample's mean and variance as a check on whether a Poisson model is plausible
607.ev: States the mean and variance of Po(λ)
607.q: If {{name}} has counts of daisies in 50 quadrats with mean 2.1 and variance 6.3, can they explain what this suggests about a Poisson model?

608.desc: Use E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p) for a binomial distribution and interpret the mean as the long-run average count
608.ev: Calculates the mean and standard deviation of B(50, 0.3)
608.q: If {{name}} knows 30% of customers buy dessert, can they work out the expected number and spread out of 50 customers?

610.desc: Use calculators, spreadsheets or tables to find areas under the normal curve and so estimate population percentages
610.ev: Finds the proportion above a value
610.q: If {{name}} knows battery lifetimes are normal with mean 500 h and SD 40 h, can they find the proportion lasting over 580 h?

612.desc: Write null and alternative hypotheses about a population parameter (e.g. H₀: p = 0.25, H₁: p > 0.25), distinguishing parameters from sample statistics
612.ev: Writes H₀ and H₁ for a context
612.q: If {{name}} wants to test a claim that a new drug helps more than 40% of patients, can they write suitable hypotheses?

603.desc: Choose a one-tailed or two-tailed test from the wording of the claim before seeing data, and split the significance level between both tails for a two-tailed test
603.ev: Decides between one and two tails from a claim
603.q: If {{name}} is testing whether a coin is biased, without saying which way, can they explain why a two-tailed test is needed?

169.desc: Count arrangements and selections using factorials, permutations and combinations, and use them to calculate probabilities
169.ev: Calculates the number of ways to arrange 5 books
169.q: If {{name}} picks 3 students from 10 for a team, can they work out how many teams are possible and whether order matters?

588.desc: Calculate P(X = r) = e^(−λ)λʳ/r! for X ~ Po(λ), by formula and with technology
588.q: If {{name}} knows a shop averages 4 customers every 10 minutes, can they find the probability that exactly 6 arrive in a 10-minute period?

598.desc: Define a random variable, build a probability distribution table and graph it, from theory or from observed frequencies
598.ev: Builds the distribution of the total of two dice
598.q: If {{name}} rolls two dice and adds them, can they build the full probability distribution of the total?

614.desc: Use a randomisation (re-allocation) simulation to judge whether a difference between two treatment groups is significant, and estimate a p-value from the simulation
614.ev: Explains why group labels are shuffled
614.q: If {{name}} finds a fertiliser group grew 3 cm taller on average, can they use a re-randomisation simulation to judge whether this could be chance?

615.desc: Sketch and describe how the shape of B(n, p) depends on n and p — symmetric when p = 0.5, skewed when p is near 0 or 1, and more bell-shaped as n grows
615.q: If {{name}} graphs B(20, 0.5) and B(20, 0.1), can they describe and explain the difference in shape?

593.desc: Explain the significance level as the threshold probability for rejecting the null hypothesis (often 5% or 1%), chosen before collecting data, and explain the effect of choosing a smaller level
593.ev: Explains what a 5% significance level means
593.q: If {{name}} is told a test used a 1% significance level, can they explain what that means and why someone might choose it?

609.desc: Calculate z-scores to compare values from different distributions and to locate values on a normal curve
609.q: If {{name}} scored 72 on a test with mean 60 and SD 8, and 80 on another with mean 75 and SD 5, can they say which result was better?

592.desc: Identify a suitable test statistic (such as the number of successes) and its distribution if the null hypothesis is true
592.ev: States the test statistic for a context
592.q: If {{name}} tests whether a dice shows six more often than it should, can they state the test statistic and its distribution under H₀?

617.desc: Decide whether a probability model is consistent with observed results, for example by simulating outcomes from a fair coin and comparing
617.q: If {{name}} spins a coin 50 times and gets 34 heads, can they use simulation to decide whether the coin is probably fair?

618.desc: Use technology to find the least-squares regression line, explain that it minimises the sum of squared residuals, and interpret its gradient and intercept in context
618.ev: Finds a regression line with technology
618.q: If {{name}} uses a calculator to find a regression line for arm span against height, can they explain what the gradient means?

611.desc: Explain the logic of a hypothesis test: assume a model (the null hypothesis), ask how surprising the data would be under it, and treat a very surprising result as evidence against the model, never as proof
611.ev: Explains why the null model is assumed true during the test
611.q: If {{name}} sees a coin land heads 16 times in 20 tosses, can they explain how a test would decide whether to doubt that it is fair?

616.desc: Recognise normally distributed data as symmetric and bell-shaped, described by mean and standard deviation, and use the 68–95–99.7 rule to estimate proportions
616.ev: Sketches a normal curve with mean and standard deviation marked
616.q: If {{name}} is told heights have mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm, can they estimate the percentage between 162 and 178 cm?

619.desc: Use x̄ to estimate μ and s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) to estimate σ², explaining why dividing by n − 1 removes the bias of dividing by n
619.q: If {{name}} has the lengths of 12 sampled bolts, can they find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance and explain the n − 1?

620.desc: Use expected values and probabilities to compare strategies and to make or judge fair decisions, such as insurance, games and random selection
620.ev: Compares two strategies by expected value
620.q: If {{name}} is offered extended warranty for a phone, can they use probabilities and costs to decide whether it's worth it?

606.desc: Calculate the variance of a discrete random variable as Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² and its standard deviation, and interpret both as measures of spread of the distribution
606.ev: Calculates E(X²) from a probability table
606.q: If {{name}} has the probability distribution for the score on a biased spinner, can they find its variance and standard deviation?

613.desc: State the conditions for a Poisson model (events occur singly, independently and at a constant average rate in a fixed interval of time or space) and decide whether a context meets them
613.ev: States the conditions for a Poisson model
613.q: If {{name}} models the number of emails arriving in an hour, can they explain what must be true for a Poisson model to be suitable?

586.desc: State the conditions for a binomial model (a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes, constant probability of success) and decide whether a context meets them
586.q: If {{name}} counts how many of 20 seeds germinate, can they explain what must be assumed for a binomial model to apply?

621.desc: Write conclusions that refer to the context, the evidence and the significance level ('there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest…'), avoiding claims that H₀ has been proved or accepted
621.q: If {{name}} reads a conclusion saying 'the test proves the coin is fair', can they explain what is wrong and rewrite it?

602.desc: Calculate a p-value as the probability, assuming H₀, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, compare it with the significance level, and avoid common misinterpretations
602.ev: Calculates a p-value from a binomial distribution
602.q: If {{name}} gets a p-value of 0.03, can they explain what it means and what it does not mean?

623.desc: Check the assumptions behind t procedures (random independent samples, approximate normality and, for a pooled test, similar variances) using plots and summary statistics, and judge how robust a conclusion is
623.ev: Checks a sample for skew and outliers before using t
623.q: If {{name}} has a small, strongly skewed sample with an outlier, can they explain whether a t-test is appropriate?

625.desc: Test whether observed frequencies fit a proposed distribution (such as a fair die or a stated ratio) by comparing observed and expected frequencies with a chi-squared statistic
625.ev: Calculates expected frequencies from a model
625.q: If {{name}} rolls a die 120 times and records the counts for each face, can they test whether the die is fair?

624.desc: Test whether two categorical variables are associated using a chi-squared test on a contingency table, calculating expected frequencies and comparing the statistic with a critical value
624.q: If {{name}} has a table of year group against preferred lunch option, can they test whether choice is independent of year group?

627.desc: Choose between binomial, Poisson, geometric and normal models for a context by identifying what is counted or measured and which assumptions are reasonable
627.q: If {{name}} is given four situations (faults per roll of cloth, heights, attempts until a pass, heads in 20 tosses), can they choose and justify a model for each?

630.desc: Choose a suitable test (binomial, normal mean, proportion, correlation or chi-squared) for a question and data type, and check the test's conditions
630.q: If {{name}} has four research questions, can they choose a suitable test for each and justify it?

633.desc: Decide whether data are paired or come from independent samples, and explain how pairing reduces variability and changes the test
633.ev: Classifies designs as paired or independent
633.q: If {{name}} is given an experiment with left and right hands of the same people, can they explain which t-test to use and why?

635.desc: Use the fact that sums and differences of independent normal variables are normal to find probabilities, such as the chance that the total mass of four items exceeds a limit
635.ev: Finds the distribution of X + Y for independent normals
635.q: If {{name}} knows the masses of apples and of the box are normally distributed, can they find the probability that a box of six apples weighs more than 1.2 kg?

636.desc: Test for a difference between two population means using z = (x̄ − ȳ)/√(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂) when the variances are known or the samples are large
636.ev: Explains where the standard error of the difference comes from
636.q: If {{name}} has large samples of journey times on two routes, can they test whether the mean times differ?

638.desc: Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a population mean as x̄ ± z·σ/√n, explaining what the confidence level means and how the interval relates to a two-tailed test
638.q: If {{name}} finds a 95% confidence interval of 12.1 to 13.5, can they explain what the 95% refers to?

640.desc: Construct and interpret a confidence interval x̄ ± t·s/√n for a population mean when σ is unknown, and explain why it is wider than the corresponding z-interval
640.q: If {{name}} has the reaction times of 9 people, can they construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

641.desc: Use P(X > r) = (1 − p)ʳ and P(X ≤ r) = 1 − (1 − p)ʳ for a geometric variable, and solve for the number of trials needed to reach a given probability
641.q: If {{name}} has a 15% chance of winning each game, can they find how many games are needed for a 90% chance of at least one win?

642.desc: Explain degrees of freedom as the number of values free to vary once constraints are fixed, why a t-test on n values uses n − 1, and how a contingency table gives (r − 1)(c − 1)
642.ev: Explains why n deviations from x̄ have n − 1 degrees of freedom
642.q: If {{name}} is told 5 numbers have mean 10, can they explain how many of the numbers can be chosen freely and link this to degrees of freedom?

634.desc: Use E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), E(X ± Y) = E(X) ± E(Y) and, for independent variables, Var(X ± Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)
634.ev: Finds the mean and variance of 3X + 2
634.q: If {{name}} knows the mean and variance of one bag's mass, can they find the mean and variance of the total mass of two independent bags, and explain why it differs from doubling one bag?

643.desc: Test the fit of a binomial or Poisson model to frequency data, estimating a parameter from the data when needed and reducing the degrees of freedom by one for each estimated parameter
643.ev: Calculates expected frequencies from a Poisson model
643.q: If {{name}} has the number of goals per match in 100 matches, can they test whether a Poisson model fits?

644.desc: Test a claim about a Poisson rate with H₀: λ = λ₀, rescaling λ₀ for the observation period and using a critical region or p-value from the Poisson distribution
644.ev: Writes hypotheses about a rate in context
644.q: If {{name}} knows a road averaged 2 accidents a month and there were 12 in the 3 months after a speed camera was installed, can they test whether the rate has changed?

628.desc: Test a claim about a population mean using z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), with critical values or p-values, for one- and two-tailed tests
628.q: If {{name}} is told a machine fills bottles to a mean of 500 ml and a sample of 30 averages 497 ml, can they test whether the mean has fallen?

645.desc: Use the individual (O − E)²/E contributions in a contingency table to describe which cells drive a significant association and in which direction
645.ev: Identifies the cells with the largest contributions
645.q: If {{name}} has found a significant association between age group and preferred news source, can they use the contributions to describe the association?

646.desc: Critique a Poisson model in context, identifying clustering, a changing rate or events that are not independent, and use a variance much larger than the mean as evidence against the model
646.ev: Identifies why a rate may not be constant
646.q: If {{name}} models goals in football matches as Poisson, can they explain which assumptions might fail and how the data could show it?

648.desc: Test a claim about a population proportion with a large sample, using a normal approximation for the sample proportion and checking that the conditions hold
648.q: If {{name}} surveys 400 voters and 54% support a policy, can they test whether support is above 50%?

649.desc: Use E(X) = 1/p and Var(X) = (1 − p)/p² for a geometric distribution and interpret the mean as the long-run average waiting time
649.ev: Calculates the expected number of trials for p = 0.25
649.q: If {{name}} knows 1 in 8 cereal boxes contains a prize, can they find the expected number of boxes needed to get the first prize?

652.desc: Explain why running many tests at 5% will produce some 'significant' results by chance, recognise p-hacking and selective reporting, and explain the role of replication
652.ev: Estimates how many false positives to expect from 20 tests
652.q: If {{name}} hears a study tested 20 foods and found one 'linked to cancer' at 5%, can they explain why this may be a false positive?

653.desc: Approximate Po(λ) by N(λ, λ) when λ is large, applying a continuity correction
653.ev: Checks that λ is large enough for the approximation
653.q: If {{name}} needs P(X > 60) for X ~ Po(50), can they use a normal approximation with a continuity correction?

647.desc: Approximate B(n, p) by N(np, np(1 − p)) when n is large and p is not too close to 0 or 1, applying a continuity correction
647.ev: Checks that a normal approximation is appropriate
647.q: If {{name}} needs P(X ≥ 60) for X ~ B(100, 0.55), can they use a normal approximation correctly?

622.desc: Test a claim about the mean of a normal population with unknown variance using t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom, for one- and two-tailed tests
622.q: If {{name}} has 10 measured fill volumes from bottles labelled 500 ml, can they test whether the mean is less than 500 ml?

631.desc: Analyse paired data (such as before-and-after measurements on the same people) by testing the mean of the differences with a one-sample t-test
631.ev: Calculates the differences and their mean and standard deviation
631.q: If {{name}} has 12 students' scores before and after a revision course, can they test whether the course improved scores on average?

654.desc: Approximate B(n, p) by Po(np) when n is large and p is small, and judge when the approximation is reasonable
654.ev: States when the approximation is appropriate
654.q: If {{name}} needs the probability that more than 3 of 1000 parts are faulty when each has a 0.2% chance of being faulty, can they use a suitable approximation?

655.desc: Explain power as the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false (1 − P(type II error)), and describe how sample size, significance level and effect size affect it
655.q: If {{name}} runs a small trial that finds 'no significant effect', can they explain why low power means this isn't strong evidence of no effect?

651.desc: Distinguish a statistically significant result from a practically important one, explaining how very large samples can make tiny effects significant
651.ev: Explains why a tiny difference can be significant with a huge sample
651.q: If {{name}} reads that a diet 'significantly' reduced weight by 0.2 kg in 10 000 people, can they explain why this might not matter?

656.desc: Use the result that if X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are independent then X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ), and recognise when the result does not apply
656.ev: Finds the distribution of the total of two independent counts
656.q: If {{name}} knows one call centre averages 3 calls a minute and another 5, can they find the probability of more than 10 calls in total in a minute?

629.desc: Test whether a population correlation coefficient ρ is zero using the sample value r and a table of critical values for the sample size and significance level
629.q: If {{name}} finds r = 0.42 from 15 pairs of data, can they test at 5% whether there is evidence of positive correlation?

637.desc: Explain that sample means vary less than individual values, that X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) for normal populations (approximately for large n), and interpret σ/√n as the standard error
637.ev: Explains why sample means vary less than individual values
637.q: If {{name}} knows individual bags of crisps vary with standard deviation 2 g, can they explain why the mean of 25 bags varies much less?

626.desc: Model the number of trials up to and including the first success with X ~ Geo(p), where P(X = r) = (1 − p)^(r − 1)p, under the same independence and constant-probability assumptions as the binomial
626.ev: Explains why the probabilities form a geometric sequence
626.q: If {{name}} rolls a die until a six appears, can they find the probability that the first six is on the fifth roll?

639.desc: Explain that when σ is estimated by s from a small sample of a normal population, (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) follows a t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails than the normal and approaches it as n grows
639.ev: Explains why replacing σ by s changes the distribution
639.q: If {{name}} has only 8 measurements and an estimated standard deviation, can they explain why a t-distribution is used instead of the normal?

632.desc: Compare the means of two independent groups with a two-sample t-test, using a pooled variance when the population variances can be assumed equal, and interpret the result for an experiment
632.ev: Calculates a pooled estimate of variance
632.q: If {{name}} has plant heights from 8 plants given a fertiliser and 10 plants without it, can they test whether the fertiliser increases mean height?

650.desc: Define type I errors (rejecting a true H₀) and type II errors (failing to reject a false H₀), find the probability of a type I error, and explain the trade-off between them
650.q: If {{name}} thinks about a medical test for a disease, can they describe a type I and a type II error and say which is worse here?

657.desc: Calculate the probability of a type I error (the actual significance level) and of a type II error for a given alternative value of λ in a Poisson test
657.ev: Finds the actual significance level of a Poisson test
657.q: If {{name}} has a critical region X ≥ 9 for testing λ = 4, can they find the probability of each type of error when the true rate is 7?

probes.q: If {{name}} calculates the gradient of y = x² between x = 3 and x = 3.1, then 3.01, can they predict the gradient at x = 3?
If {{name}} needs to differentiate 3/√x, can they rewrite it as a power and differentiate it?
If {{name}} has y = x³ − 3x² + 2, can they find and classify its stationary points?

689.desc: Find antiderivatives (indefinite integrals) of powers of x by reversing differentiation, including the constant of integration
689.q: If {{name}} is asked which functions have derivative 6x², can they find them all?

691.desc: Define a function as continuous at a point when its limit equals its value there, and identify jumps, holes and asymptotes as discontinuities
691.q: If {{name}} sees a graph of parking charges that jumps at each hour, can they explain why it is not continuous?

693.desc: Use and interpret dy/dx, f′(x), d/dx and d²y/dx², and read them as rates of change with units
693.q: If {{name}} sees dV/dt = −3 for a leaking tank, can they explain in words, with units, what it means?

694.desc: Interpret derivatives as rates of change in contexts such as marginal cost, population growth and flow rates, with units
694.ev: Interprets C′(100) for a cost function
694.q: If {{name}} is told P′(10) = 250 for a town's population in years, can they explain what that means?

695.desc: Use the inverse relationship with eˣ to show d/dx(ln x) = 1/x, and differentiate logarithmic expressions
695.q: If {{name}} needs to differentiate ln(x²), can they simplify first and get the same answer?

696.desc: Differentiate xⁿ for any rational n, including negative and fractional powers, after rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers
696.q: If {{name}} needs to differentiate 3/√x, can they rewrite it as a power and differentiate it?

698.desc: Differentiate sin x and cos x (in radians), explaining from the graphs why the derivative of sin is cos and why radians are needed
698.q: If {{name}} sketches y = sin x and its gradient graph, can they explain why the derivative is cos x?

688.desc: Use the sum and constant-multiple rules to differentiate polynomials and other sums of powers
688.q: If {{name}} has y = 2x³ − 5x + 7, can they find the gradient of the curve at x = 2?

702.desc: Find velocity from acceleration and displacement from velocity by integration, using initial conditions, and distinguish displacement from total distance
702.q: If {{name}} knows a car's velocity is v = 3t² − 12 m/s, can they find its displacement and total distance in the first 4 s?

499.desc: Find the equations of the tangent and normal to a curve at a given point using the derivative and perpendicular gradients
499.ev: Finds the gradient at a point
499.q: If {{name}} has the curve y = x² − 3x at the point (4, 4), can they find the equation of the tangent there?

704.desc: Approximate areas under curves with rectangles and with the trapezium rule, and explain how more strips improve the estimate
704.ev: Estimates an area with four rectangles
704.q: If {{name}} estimates the area under y = x² from 0 to 2 with four strips, can they say whether the answer is an over- or underestimate?

699.desc: Evaluate definite integrals of polynomials using [F(x)] with limits, and interpret the result as signed area
699.q: If {{name}} evaluates ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx and gets 0, can they explain why even though there is area under the curve?

707.desc: Estimate the gradient of a curve at a point by calculating gradients of chords over shrinking intervals, and explain the tangent gradient as the limit of these chord gradients
707.ev: Calculates chord gradients for intervals of 1, 0.1 and 0.01
707.q: If {{name}} calculates the gradient of y = x² between x = 3 and x = 3.1, then 3.01, can they predict the gradient at x = 3?

708.desc: Use the sign of the derivative to find intervals where a function is increasing or decreasing
708.ev: Finds where a cubic is increasing
708.q: If {{name}} has f(x) = x³ − 12x, can they find where the function is decreasing?

151.desc: Describe the behaviour of functions as x grows without bound, including horizontal asymptotes of rational and exponential functions
151.ev: Finds the limit of (2x + 1)/x as x → ∞
151.q: If {{name}} looks at y = 1/x for very large x, can they explain what value y approaches and why it never reaches it?

690.desc: Understand a limit as the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point, estimate limits from tables and graphs, and handle cases like (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at x = 1
690.ev: Estimates a limit from a table of values
690.q: If {{name}} sees that (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at x = 1, can they still find what value it approaches?

709.desc: Locate roots by a change of sign on a continuous function and refine them with iteration or the Newton–Raphson method
709.ev: Shows a root lies between 1 and 2 by change of sign
709.q: If {{name}} needs a root of x³ − 2x − 5 = 0, can they show where it is and find it to 3 decimal places?

703.desc: Generalise from distance under a velocity–time graph to any rate: the signed area under a rate graph gives the net change in the quantity (water in a tank, money in an account, people in a building), with area below the axis counting as decrease
703.ev: Finds the net change in water from an in/out flow-rate graph
703.q: If {{name}} sees a graph of water flowing into a tank in litres per minute, can they explain how to find the total water added?

712.desc: Set up a function for a quantity to maximise or minimise from a context, differentiate, solve and check the answer is a maximum or minimum that makes sense
712.ev: Forms an expression for the volume of an open box
712.q: If {{name}} cuts squares from the corners of a sheet of card to make an open box, can they find the cut that gives the largest volume?

697.desc: Sketch the graph of f′(x) from the graph of f(x) by reading where the gradient is positive, negative and zero
697.ev: Marks where the gradient is zero
697.q: If {{name}} is shown a graph with a hill and a valley, can they sketch the graph of its gradient?

711.desc: Find stationary points by solving f′(x) = 0 and classify them by the sign of the gradient either side
711.q: If {{name}} has y = x³ − 3x² + 2, can they find and classify its stationary points?

701.desc: Explain why integrals include + C, and use a known point or initial value to find C
701.ev: Explains why many functions share the same derivative
701.q: If {{name}} knows dy/dx = 2x and the curve passes through (1, 5), can they find the equation of the curve?

713.desc: Define the definite integral as the limit of sums of strips as their width tends to zero, and use ∫ notation with limits
713.ev: Explains the integral as a limit of sums
713.q: If {{name}} sees ∫₀³ x² dx, can they explain what it means as a limit of rectangles?

692.desc: Define the derivative as the limit of [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h as h → 0 and use it to differentiate simple polynomials
692.q: If {{name}} is asked to prove that the derivative of x² is 2x, can they do it from first principles?

188.desc: Explain that e is the base for which the gradient of eˣ equals its value, so d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, and differentiate e^(kx)
188.q: If {{name}} sees that the gradient of y = eˣ at any point equals y, can they explain what that means for growth?

705.desc: Explain the fundamental theorem of calculus — that differentiation and integration are inverse processes — and use it to evaluate definite integrals with antiderivatives
705.q: If {{name}} is asked why ∫₀² x² dx can be found from x³/3 rather than by adding rectangles, can they explain the link?

714.desc: Find second derivatives and use their sign to classify stationary points as maxima or minima, interpreting d²y/dx² as a rate of change of gradient
714.q: If {{name}} finds a stationary point where d²y/dx² = −6, can they say whether it's a maximum or minimum and why?

700.desc: Find velocity and acceleration by differentiating displacement with respect to time, and interpret signs and stationary values
700.q: If {{name}} has s = t³ − 6t² + 9t for a moving particle, can they find when it is momentarily at rest?

717.desc: Compare truncated series with the true function graphically and numerically, seeing that accuracy improves with more terms and near the centre of expansion
717.ev: Graphs successive approximations to sin x
717.q: If {{name}} graphs 1, 1 + x and 1 + x + x²/2 against eˣ, can they describe where each is accurate?

719.desc: Approximate a function near a point by a polynomial whose value and derivatives match there, starting from the tangent line and adding a quadratic term
719.ev: Finds a quadratic matching f, f′ and f″ at x = 0
719.q: If {{name}} graphs cos x near 0, can they find a quadratic that fits it better than the tangent line?

721.desc: Find the length of a curve with s = ∫√(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx, or the parametric form, and use the catenary as a case where 1 + sinh²x = cosh²x makes the integral simple
721.ev: Explains the formula from small right-angled triangles
721.q: If {{name}} needs the length of the curve y = cosh x between x = 0 and x = 1, can they set up and evaluate the integral?

722.desc: Derive the area formula A = ½∫r²dθ by adding thin sectors of area ½r²δθ, and set up area integrals for polar regions
722.ev: Explains the formula as a sum of thin sectors
722.q: If {{name}} wants the area inside one loop of a polar curve, can they explain where ½∫r²dθ comes from?

725.desc: Show that an ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area πab, by parametric integration or by stretching a circle
725.ev: Sets up a parametric integral for the area of an ellipse
725.q: If {{name}} is given x²/16 + y²/9 = 1, can they find the area of the ellipse and justify the formula?

723.desc: Find the area under a parametric curve using ∫ y (dx/dt) dt, changing the limits to values of t
723.ev: Sets up the integral in terms of t
723.q: If {{name}} needs the area under x = t², y = 2t from x = 0 to x = 4, can they set up and evaluate the integral in t?

728.desc: Find areas under hyperbolic curves and volumes of revolution such as y = cosh x rotated about the x-axis, using hyperbolic identities to integrate squares
728.ev: Finds the area under y = sinh x between two limits
728.q: If {{name}} rotates y = cosh x from 0 to 1 about the x-axis, can they find the exact volume?

729.desc: Find areas between a curve and a line or between two curves by finding intersections and integrating the difference
729.q: If {{name}} needs the area between y = x² and y = x + 2, can they set up and evaluate the integral?

731.desc: Find the area of a region inside one polar curve and outside another, using intersections to find the limits
731.ev: Finds the limits from the points of intersection
731.q: If {{name}} has r = 3 cos θ and r = 1 + cos θ, can they find the area inside the first curve but outside the second?

732.desc: Calculate the average value of a function over an interval as the integral divided by the interval width
732.ev: Calculates the average of x² on [0, 3]
732.q: If {{name}} has a model for temperature through the day, can they find the average temperature between 6 am and 6 pm?

734.desc: Find series for new functions by substituting into, multiplying, differentiating or integrating known Maclaurin series
734.ev: Finds the series for e^(2x) by substitution
734.q: If {{name}} knows the series for eˣ, can they quickly write the series for e^(−x²)?

730.desc: Calculate areas enclosed by polar curves, such as the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ) with area 3πa²/2 or one petal of a rose curve
730.ev: Calculates the area enclosed by a cardioid
730.q: If {{name}} is given r = 2(1 + cos θ), can they find the area it encloses?

735.desc: Derive d/dx(arcsin x) = 1/√(1 − x²) and d/dx(arctan x) = 1/(1 + x²), and use the related integrals of 1/√(a² − x²) and 1/(a² + x²)
735.ev: Derives the derivative of arcsin x by implicit differentiation
735.q: If {{name}} needs the integral of 1/√(4 − x²) from 0 to 1, can they find its exact value?

738.desc: Decide which rules a function needs and apply them in the right order, checking by simplifying or with technology
738.ev: Identifies which rules an expression needs
738.q: If {{name}} sees y = x² e^(3x), can they plan which rules to use before starting?

740.desc: Compare a sum with an integral using rectangles, for example bounding 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n with ln n to explain why the harmonic series diverges
740.ev: Draws rectangles comparing a sum with an area
740.q: If {{name}} draws rectangles under y = 1/x, can they explain why the harmonic series grows like ln n?

741.desc: Describe concave up and down sections of a curve and find points of inflection where concavity changes
741.ev: Identifies concave regions on a graph
741.q: If {{name}} sees a graph of an epidemic's total cases, can they find where new cases stopped speeding up?

742.desc: Use the chain rule to link rates of change of related quantities, such as how fast the radius of a balloon grows when its volume increases at a known rate
742.q: If {{name}} pumps air into a balloon at 50 cm³/s, can they find how fast the radius grows when it is 10 cm?

743.desc: Combine intercepts, stationary points, concavity and end behaviour to sketch curves accurately without technology
743.ev: Sketches a cubic with all key features labelled
743.q: If {{name}} is given y = x⁴ − 4x², can they sketch the graph showing all key features?

748.desc: Use differential equations to model physical processes such as radioactive decay, capacitor discharge and falling with air resistance, interpreting terminal values
748.ev: Writes a DE for radioactive decay
748.q: If {{name}} writes a model for a skydiver with drag, can they explain from the equation why the speed levels off?

749.desc: Differentiate sinh x, cosh x and tanh x (giving cosh x, sinh x and sech²x) from their exponential definitions, and combine them with the chain, product and quotient rules
749.ev: Derives d/dx(cosh x) = sinh x from the definition
749.q: If {{name}} needs dy/dx for y = x² cosh 2x, can they differentiate it correctly?

750.desc: Derive and use d/dx(arsinh x) = 1/√(x² + 1), d/dx(arcosh x) = 1/√(x² − 1) and d/dx(artanh x) = 1/(1 − x²)
750.ev: Derives the derivative of arsinh x by implicit differentiation
750.q: If {{name}} needs d/dx of arsinh(x/3), can they find it and simplify the answer?

752.desc: Approximate solutions to differential equations step by step with Euler's method in a spreadsheet, and explain how step size affects accuracy
752.ev: Carries out three Euler steps by hand
752.q: If {{name}} uses Euler's method with step 0.1 and then 0.01, can they explain which result is more accurate and why?

744.desc: Solve dy/dt = ky to obtain y = y₀e^(kt), and use it for growth and decay problems such as populations and radioactive decay
744.q: If {{name}} knows a population grows at a rate proportional to its size and doubles in 5 years, can they find the model?

755.desc: Integrate expressions containing √(a² + x²) or √(x² − a²) by substituting x = a sinh u or x = a cosh u and simplifying with hyperbolic identities
755.q: If {{name}} needs the integral of √(x² + 4), can they choose a substitution and complete the integration?

500.desc: Differentiate relations such as x² + y² = 25 implicitly with respect to x and find gradients at points
500.q: If {{name}} has the circle x² + y² = 25, can they find the gradient at (3, 4) without solving for y?

754.desc: Use ∫1/√(x² + a²) dx = arsinh(x/a) + c and ∫1/√(x² − a²) dx = arcosh(x/a) + c, completing the square where needed, and give definite answers in logarithmic form
754.q: If {{name}} needs the integral of 1/√(x² − 9) from 3 to 5, can they give the exact answer as a logarithm?

739.desc: Integrate exponential, reciprocal and trigonometric functions using the reverse of their derivatives
739.q: If {{name}} needs ∫ (eˣ + 1/x) dx, can they find it and check by differentiating?

720.desc: Integrate sinh, cosh and sech² and use identities such as cosh²x = ½(cosh 2x + 1) to integrate powers and products of hyperbolic functions
720.q: If {{name}} needs the integral of cosh²x from 0 to 1, can they choose an identity and evaluate it?

724.desc: Integrate sin²θ, cos²θ and sin θ cos θ by rewriting them with double-angle formulae, as needed for polar areas
724.ev: Integrates cos²θ using cos²θ = ½(1 + cos 2θ)
724.q: If {{name}} needs to find the integral of sin²θ from 0 to π, can they choose an identity that makes it integrable?

756.desc: Integrate rational functions by splitting them into partial fractions, giving answers in terms of logarithms
756.q: If {{name}} needs ∫ 3/((x − 1)(x + 2)) dx, can they split it and integrate?

757.desc: Integrate products using integration by parts, choosing u and dv/dx sensibly
757.q: If {{name}} needs ∫ x cos x dx, can they choose u and integrate it?

726.desc: Integrate by substitution, recognising the reverse chain rule pattern f′(g(x))g′(x)
726.ev: Spots the reverse chain rule pattern
726.q: If {{name}} sees ∫ x e^(x²) dx, can they choose a substitution and integrate it?

716.desc: Derive Maclaurin series from derivatives at 0, f(x) = f(0) + f′(0)x + f″(0)x²/2! + …, and know the series for eˣ, sin x, cos x and ln(1 + x)
716.q: If {{name}} is asked to find a series for eˣ, can they derive it from the derivatives at 0?

758.desc: Find the Maclaurin series of sinh x and cosh x, and compare them with the series for sin x, cos x and eˣ
758.ev: Derives the series for cosh x by repeated differentiation
758.q: If {{name}} is asked for the first three non-zero terms of the series for cosh 2x, can they find them?

759.desc: Solve dv/dt = g(1 − v²/V²) for a falling object with quadratic air resistance to get v = V tanh(gt/V), and interpret the approach to terminal velocity
759.ev: Separates variables and integrates using partial fractions or artanh
759.q: If {{name}} models a skydiver with air resistance proportional to v², can they show the speed approaches a terminal value and find it?

761.desc: Model cooling with dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ), solve it, and fit the model to experimental cooling data
761.q: If {{name}} records a cup of tea cooling, can they use Newton's law of cooling to predict when it reaches 40 °C?

501.desc: Find dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) for a parametric curve and use it to find tangents, normals and stationary points
501.ev: Finds dy/dx for x = t², y = t³
501.q: If {{name}} is given a curve in terms of t, can they find the gradient at t = 2 without converting to Cartesian form?

762.desc: Recognise that some Maclaurin series converge for all x (eˣ, sin x) while others converge only on an interval (ln(1 + x) for −1 < x ≤ 1, 1/(1 − x) for |x| < 1)
762.ev: States the range of validity of standard series
762.q: If {{name}} uses the series for ln(1 + x) at x = 3, can they explain why the answer is nonsense?

753.desc: Solve first-order separable differential equations by separating variables and integrating, using an initial condition
753.q: If {{name}} has dy/dx = 2xy with y = 3 when x = 0, can they solve it?

751.desc: Sketch and read slope fields for first-order differential equations and draw solution curves through given points
751.ev: Draws short gradient segments at grid points
751.q: If {{name}} is given the slope field for dy/dx = x − y, can they sketch the solution through (0, 1)?

718.desc: Use the tangent line to approximate function values near a point, and estimate small changes with δy ≈ (dy/dx) δx
718.q: If {{name}} needs √26 without a calculator, can they use the tangent to y = √x at x = 25?

764.desc: Find points on a polar curve where the tangent is parallel or perpendicular to the initial line by solving dy/dθ = 0 or dx/dθ = 0 for x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ
764.ev: Finds where the tangent to a cardioid is parallel to the initial line
764.q: If {{name}} is given r = 1 + cos θ, can they find the points where the tangent is parallel to the initial line?

765.desc: Find Taylor series about x = a, such as ln x about x = 1, and use them to approximate values near a
765.ev: Finds the series for ln x about x = 1
765.q: If {{name}} needs ln 1.1, can they use a series about x = 1 rather than about 0?

733.desc: Differentiate composite functions using the chain rule, dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx
733.q: If {{name}} needs to differentiate √(1 + x²), can they identify the inner function and apply the chain rule?

736.desc: Differentiate products of functions using d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx
736.q: If {{name}} has y = x³ ln x, can they differentiate it with the product rule?

737.desc: Differentiate quotients of functions using the quotient rule and simplify the result
737.q: If {{name}} has y = x²/(x + 1), can they differentiate it and simplify?

766.desc: Use truncated series to estimate values such as e^0.1, to justify small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2), and to find limits such as (sin x)/x as x → 0
766.ev: Estimates e^0.1 from the first terms
766.q: If {{name}} needs the limit of (1 − cos x)/x² as x → 0, can they use series to find it?

727.desc: Find volumes of solids formed by rotating a region about the x-axis using V = π∫y² dx
727.ev: Sets up the integral for a rotated curve
727.q: If {{name}} rotates y = √x from 0 to 4 about the x-axis, can they find the volume of the solid?

763.desc: Interpret a differential equation as a statement about how a quantity changes, form simple ones from descriptions, and check whether a function is a solution
763.ev: Writes dP/dt = kP for 'growth proportional to population'
763.q: If {{name}} reads that 'a rumour spreads at a rate proportional to the number who know it', can they write that as a differential equation?

770.desc: Calculate work done by a varying force as the area under a force–distance graph, W = ∫F dx, including the energy stored in a spring
770.ev: Finds the work done stretching a spring
770.q: If {{name}} knows a spring's force is F = 200x, can they work out the energy stored when it's stretched 0.1 m?

probes.q: If {{name}} saw the formula H₂O on a label, could they explain what it means — which atoms are involved, how many of each, and why water is a compound rather than just a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen?
If {{name}} draws a water molecule, can they show which electrons are shared between the oxygen and the two hydrogens?
If {{name}} is shown the structures of ethanol, ethanoic acid and ethene, can they circle the functional group in each and name the family?

774.desc: Explain the differences between atoms, elements, and compounds; describe the simple Bohr model of the atom (nucleus with protons and neutrons, electrons in shells); and write and interpret chemical symbols and simple formulae
774.ev: Defines atom, element, and compound and distinguishes between them with examples
774.q: If {{name}} saw the formula H₂O on a label, could they explain what it means — which atoms are involved, how many of each, and why water is a compound rather than just a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen?

776.desc: Explain diffusion — the spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration — as a result of random particle motion, and explain why it is fastest in gases and in warmer conditions
776.ev: Defines diffusion as net movement from high to low concentration
776.q: If someone opens a bottle of perfume at one end of a room, can {{name}} explain why people at the other end smell it a little later, using the idea of moving particles?

779.desc: Explain melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, and sublimation using the particle model, interpreting heating and cooling curves to identify melting and boiling points
779.ev: Describes what happens to particles during each change of state
779.q: If {{name}} was heating a block of ice in a pan and drew a graph of temperature over time, could they explain why the line goes flat at certain points — and what's happening to the particles when it does?

781.desc: Compare the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals, explaining metallic properties (malleability, lustre, conductivity) and how position in the periodic table predicts reactivity
781.ev: Lists physical properties typical of metals (shiny, malleable, good conductor) and non-metals
781.q: If {{name}} had an unknown substance that was shiny, could be bent without breaking, and conducted electricity, could they identify it as likely a metal and explain how each property points to that conclusion?

785.desc: Distinguish between physical changes (reversible, no new substances formed) and chemical changes (new substances formed, often irreversible), using conservation of mass to understand both types
785.ev: Classifies given changes as physical or chemical with justification
785.q: If {{name}} dissolved sugar in tea versus burnt toast in the toaster, could they explain which is a physical change and which is a chemical change — and what test would show that mass is conserved in both cases?

786.desc: Distinguish between pure substances and mixtures, identify formulations as useful mixtures with precise compositions, and use melting and boiling points to test for purity
786.ev: Explains why a pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point but a mixture melts over a range
786.q: If {{name}} was checking whether a sample of water was pure, could they explain one test they could do — and say what result would tell them it was definitely pure versus a mixture?

788.desc: Select and carry out appropriate separation techniques for different types of mixtures: filtration (insoluble solids), distillation (liquids by boiling point), crystallisation (dissolved solids), and chromatography (coloured substances)
788.ev: Selects the correct separation technique for a given mixture with justification
788.q: If {{name}} needed to separate salt from sand mixed together in water, could they describe two stages of separation, the equipment needed, and explain why each step works?

773.desc: Use the particle model to explain the properties of solids, liquids, and gases — including differences in arrangement, movement, and spacing — and apply the model to explain density, compressibility, and the anomalous expansion of water
773.ev: Draws particle diagrams for solids, liquids, and gases showing correct arrangement and spacing
773.q: If {{name}} was asked why you can squash a balloon but not a water bottle full of liquid, could they explain using the idea of particles what's different about gases and liquids?

780.desc: Describe the organisation of the periodic table into periods and groups, explain the contribution of Mendeleev, and use the table to identify metals, non-metals, and predict patterns in reactivity
780.ev: Explains why the periodic table is arranged into periods (rows) and groups (columns)
780.q: If {{name}} was looking at a periodic table, could they explain why elements in the same column tend to behave similarly — and say what Mendeleev did that made it so useful to chemists?

793.desc: Describe and write word equations for the reactions of acids with metals, alkalis (neutralisation), and metal oxides/hydroxides, identifying the salt produced in each case
793.ev: Writes word equations for: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + metal oxide → salt + water
793.q: If {{name}} was asked how an indigestion tablet works to relieve stomach acid, could they explain what type of chemical reaction is happening and write a simple word equation for it?

791.desc: Define acids and alkalis in terms of hydrogen ion concentration, describe the pH scale (0–14), and explain how indicators are used to identify and measure acidity or alkalinity
791.ev: States that acids have pH below 7, alkalis have pH above 7, and neutral is pH 7
791.q: If {{name}} used a piece of universal indicator paper to test lemon juice and baking soda solution, could they predict what colour each would turn and explain what that tells you about each substance?

431.desc: Calculate density using density = mass ÷ volume, measure the density of regular and irregular objects (by displacement), and use particle spacing to explain why gases are far less dense than solids and liquids
431.ev: Calculates density from mass and volume with correct units (g/cm³ or kg/m³)
431.q: If {{name}} has a 50 g pebble that pushes the water level in a measuring cylinder up by 20 cm³, can they work out the pebble's density and say whether it will float?

796.desc: Describe the atom as a tiny positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons, and give the relative charge and relative mass of each particle
796.ev: Gives relative charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
796.q: If {{name}} is asked why an atom with 6 protons isn't positively charged overall, can they explain the role of the electrons?

797.desc: Count the atoms of each element in chemical formulae and equations, correctly handling subscripts, brackets and the large numbers (coefficients) written in front of formulae
797.ev: Counts atoms of each element in formulae such as H₂SO₄ and Ca(OH)₂
797.q: If {{name}} sees the formula H₂SO₄, can they say which elements are in it and how many atoms of each there are?

800.desc: Describe the composition of Earth's atmosphere (mainly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of CO₂ and other gases), explain how human activity increases CO₂, and describe the impact on global climate
800.ev: States the approximate percentages of nitrogen, oxygen, CO₂, and argon in the atmosphere
800.q: If {{name}} was asked why scientists are worried about CO₂ levels rising, could they explain what CO₂ does in the atmosphere, why human activities produce more of it, and what effects it's having on the planet?

803.desc: Explain that during evaporation the fastest-moving particles escape from the surface of a liquid, lowering the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind — which is why sweating and wet skin cool us down
803.ev: Distinguishes evaporation (at the surface, any temperature) from boiling (throughout, at the boiling point)
803.q: If {{name}} gets out of a swimming pool on a windy day and feels cold, can they explain why the evaporating water makes their skin cooler?

805.desc: Explain that many raw materials (metals, fossil fuels, minerals) are finite resources, describe the environmental costs of extraction, and evaluate the benefits of recycling and the circular economy
805.ev: Identifies examples of finite natural resources and explains why they are finite
805.q: If {{name}} was deciding whether to recycle an aluminium drinks can or throw it away, could they explain what goes into making new aluminium from scratch — and why recycling it uses much less energy?

806.desc: Explain gas pressure as the result of gas particles colliding with the walls of their container, and predict how pressure changes when the gas is heated, compressed or more gas is added
806.ev: Explains that pressure comes from many particle collisions with the container walls
806.q: If {{name}} pumps up a bike tyre, can they explain what the air particles inside are doing to make the tyre feel harder?

808.desc: Distinguish between exothermic reactions (release energy, temperature rises) and endothermic reactions (absorb energy, temperature falls), with everyday and industrial examples
808.ev: Defines exothermic and endothermic in terms of energy transfer to and from the surroundings
808.q: If {{name}} shook a sports cold pack to activate it and it got cold, or lit a match and it got hot, could they explain what type of reaction is happening in each case and why one gets hot while the other gets cold?

809.desc: Explain that in a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged into new substances but none are created or destroyed, using particle diagrams of reactants and products to show why total mass is conserved
809.ev: Draws before-and-after particle diagrams with the same atoms
809.q: If {{name}} draws a particle picture of hydrogen and oxygen making water, can they show that every atom at the start is still there at the end?

802.desc: Explain that particles in every substance are constantly moving, and that the temperature of a substance is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles — hotter means faster-moving (or more strongly vibrating) particles
802.ev: States that particles move faster on average when a substance is heated
802.q: If {{name}} drops food colouring into a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water, can they explain — using moving particles — why it spreads faster in the hot one?

804.desc: Order common metals in the reactivity series and explain how a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one; describe how carbon is used to extract metals from their oxides in industry
804.ev: Recalls the order of common metals in the reactivity series (potassium to gold)
804.q: If {{name}} was asked why humans used gold and copper before iron and aluminium, could they explain how a metal's reactivity determines how easy it is to extract — and why carbon can extract some metals but not others?

813.desc: Explain the rock cycle: how igneous rocks form from magma, sedimentary rocks from compressed sediment, and metamorphic rocks from heat and pressure, and how all rock types can transform into one another over geological time
813.ev: Describes how each rock type (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) is formed
813.q: If {{name}} picked up a piece of marble on a school trip, could they explain how it was originally limestone, what changed it into marble, and how long that process took?

792.desc: Identify and describe four types of chemical reaction: combustion (burning in oxygen), oxidation (gain of oxygen), thermal decomposition (breaking down by heat), and displacement (more reactive metal replaces less reactive one)
792.ev: Writes a word equation for each type of reaction with an example
792.q: If {{name}} saw iron going rusty and a candle burning, could they explain what type of chemical reaction is happening in each case — and write a simple word equation for one of them?

814.desc: Explain the shape of temperature–time graphs for a substance being heated or cooled: on the sloping sections energy speeds up particles (temperature rises), while on the flat sections energy is used to overcome the attractions between particles and change their arrangement, so temperature stays constant until the change of state is complete
814.ev: Identifies melting and boiling points from the flat sections of a heating curve
814.q: If {{name}} is shown a graph of ice being heated until it boils, can they point to where it is melting and explain why the line goes flat there?

815.desc: Write and interpret word equations for chemical reactions, identifying reactants and products and using the arrow to mean 'react to form'
815.ev: Writes a word equation for a described reaction
815.q: If {{name}} sees magnesium burning brightly to make a white powder, can they write a word equation for what happened?

816.desc: Use atomic number (number of protons) and mass number (protons + neutrons) to work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom from its nuclear symbol
816.ev: Reads atomic and mass numbers from a nuclear symbol or periodic table
816.q: If {{name}} sees sodium written as ²³₁₁Na, can they work out how many protons, neutrons and electrons a sodium atom has?

817.desc: Balance symbol equations by changing only the numbers in front of formulae so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides
817.ev: Balances equations such as Mg + O₂ → MgO and CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
817.q: If {{name}} is given H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, can they balance it and explain why they can't just change H₂O to H₂O₂?

818.desc: Describe the properties and uses of ceramics (hard, brittle, heat-resistant), polymers (flexible, lightweight, variable), and composites (combine properties of constituent materials), giving real-world examples of each
818.ev: Gives the key properties of ceramics, polymers, and composites with examples of each
818.q: If {{name}} was looking at a racing bicycle made of carbon fibre, could they explain why neither carbon nor plastic alone would work as well — and what makes the combination a composite better than either material on its own?

819.desc: Describe complete combustion of hydrocarbon fuels to carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion producing carbon monoxide and soot, and why incomplete combustion is dangerous
819.ev: Writes a word and symbol equation for the complete combustion of methane
819.q: If {{name}} sees a gas flame burning yellow and sooty instead of blue, can they explain what is different about how the fuel is burning and why it matters?

820.desc: Design, test and refine a device that uses an exothermic or endothermic process to warm or cool, choosing amounts of substances and measuring temperature change to evaluate the design
820.ev: Chooses an exothermic or endothermic reaction suitable for the purpose
820.q: If {{name}} is asked to make an instant cold pack for a sports injury, can they choose a suitable reaction and describe how they'd test which mix works best?

822.desc: Trace how evidence changed the model of the atom — Dalton's solid spheres, Thomson's plum pudding, Rutherford's gold-foil experiment revealing the nucleus, Bohr's electron shells and Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
822.ev: Puts the main atomic models in historical order
822.q: If {{name}} hears that most alpha particles went straight through gold foil but a few bounced back, can they explain what this told Rutherford about the atom?

823.desc: Explain why mass seems to change when a reaction happens in an open container (a gas escapes or is gained from the air) but stays the same in a sealed container
823.ev: Predicts the mass change when a gas is produced in an open flask
823.q: If {{name}} weighs a fizzing tablet dissolving in an open cup and sees the mass go down, can they explain why mass hasn't really been destroyed?

824.desc: Evaluate the simple particle model: recognise what it explains well (states, diffusion, pressure) and what it leaves out — particles are not hard coloured spheres, there are forces between them, and real particles are atoms, ions or molecules of different sizes
824.ev: Names two things the particle model explains well
824.q: If {{name}} is shown a textbook particle diagram of a gas, can they say one thing it gets right and one way real gas particles are different from the picture?

825.desc: Appreciate the scale of atoms (about 10⁻¹⁰ m across) and nuclei (about 10⁻¹⁴ to 10⁻¹⁵ m), using scientific notation and analogies to show that an atom is mostly empty space
825.ev: Writes the size of an atom in scientific notation
825.q: If {{name}} is told an atom is about 0.0000000001 m across, can they write that in scientific notation and describe how small the nucleus is by comparison?

827.desc: Describe the properties and reactions of the alkali metals with water and oxygen, and explain why reactivity increases down the group using distance of the outer electron from the nucleus
827.ev: Describes lithium, sodium and potassium reacting with water and names the products
827.q: If {{name}} has seen lithium fizz gently in water and potassium burst into flame, can they predict what rubidium would do and explain why?

830.desc: Identify alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and name and draw the first four (methane, ethane, propane, butane)
830.ev: Names and draws methane to butane
830.q: If {{name}} is asked for the formula of the alkane with 10 carbon atoms, can they work it out and explain why it is called saturated?

833.desc: Identify alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a C=C double bond with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, and name and draw ethene, propene and butene
833.ev: Draws ethene and propene showing the double bond
833.q: If {{name}} is shown C₃H₈ and C₃H₆, can they say which is an alkene and draw it?

834.desc: Write balanced symbol equations for the complete combustion of any alkane, including larger alkanes that need fractional or doubled coefficients, and use the general formula to predict the oxygen needed
834.ev: Balances the complete combustion of propane
834.q: If {{name}} writes the equation for burning butane, can they balance the oxygen without leaving a fraction?

835.desc: Explain that reactions happen only when particles collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy), so the rate depends on the frequency and energy of collisions
835.ev: States the two conditions for a successful collision
835.q: If {{name}} is asked why food goes off more slowly in the fridge, can they explain using collisions between particles?

832.desc: Explain covalent bonding as a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms, and draw dot-and-cross and displayed diagrams for simple molecules such as H₂, H₂O, CH₄ and CO₂
832.ev: Draws dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules
832.q: If {{name}} draws a water molecule, can they show which electrons are shared between the oxygen and the two hydrogens?

838.desc: Explain that cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes using heat and a catalyst or steam, write balanced cracking equations, and explain why it is needed to match supply with demand
838.q: If {{name}} sees that refineries produce more heavy fractions than people buy, can they explain how cracking helps and write an equation for it?

839.desc: Describe crude oil as a mixture of many hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine organisms, and explain why it is a finite resource
839.q: If {{name}} is told crude oil is 'running out', can they explain how it formed and why it can't be replaced on a human timescale?

836.desc: Write electron configurations for the first 20 elements using the 2, 8, 8 filling pattern and draw shell diagrams, linking the number of outer-shell electrons to the element's position
836.ev: Writes configurations such as 2,8,1 for sodium
836.q: If {{name}} is told magnesium has 12 electrons, can they draw how those electrons are arranged in shells?

841.desc: Explain that atoms become ions by losing or gaining electrons to achieve a full outer shell, predict the charge on simple ions from group number, and draw ions with square brackets and charges
841.ev: Predicts ion charges for groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
841.q: If {{name}} is asked what happens to a magnesium atom when it forms an ion, can they say how many electrons it loses and what charge it ends up with?

837.desc: Explain how crude oil is separated into fractions in a fractionating column with a temperature gradient, where hydrocarbons condense at different heights according to boiling point, and name uses of the main fractions
837.ev: Describes the temperature gradient in the column
837.q: If {{name}} sees a diagram of a fractionating column, can they explain why petrol comes out near the top and bitumen at the bottom?

843.desc: Describe the halogens' physical trends and displacement reactions, and explain why reactivity decreases down the group because it becomes harder to gain an electron
843.ev: Describes colour and state trend from fluorine to iodine
843.q: If {{name}} adds chlorine water to potassium bromide solution, can they predict what happens and explain why chlorine wins?

831.desc: Explain that a homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, where successive members differ by CH₂, with similar chemical properties and gradually changing physical properties
831.ev: States the features of a homologous series
831.q: If {{name}} is told about a family of compounds that all react the same way but have steadily rising boiling points, can they explain what makes it a homologous series?

828.desc: Define a hydrocarbon as a compound of hydrogen and carbon only, and distinguish hydrocarbons from other carbon compounds such as ethanol or glucose
828.ev: Defines a hydrocarbon correctly, including the word 'only'
828.q: If {{name}} sees the formulae CH₄, C₂H₅OH and C₃H₆, can they pick out the hydrocarbons and explain why?

845.desc: Explain ionic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice, and use this to explain high melting points and conductivity when molten or dissolved
845.ev: Draws a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride
845.q: If {{name}} is asked why salt has to be melted or dissolved before it conducts electricity, can they explain what the ions need to be able to do?

846.desc: Explain that isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers but almost identical chemical properties
846.q: If {{name}} is told about carbon-12 and carbon-14, can they explain what is the same and what is different about these two kinds of carbon atom?

829.desc: Represent organic molecules with molecular formulae (C₂H₆), condensed structural formulae (CH₃CH₃) and displayed formulae showing every bond, and convert between them
829.ev: Writes the molecular formula from a displayed formula
829.q: If {{name}} is given the displayed formula of a molecule, can they write its molecular and structural formulae?

840.desc: Explain that the noble gases are unreactive because their outer shell is full, and use this to explain why other atoms tend to lose, gain or share electrons
840.ev: Explains noble-gas unreactivity in terms of a full outer shell
840.q: If {{name}} is asked why balloons are filled with helium rather than hydrogen, can they connect helium's safety to its electron arrangement?

826.desc: Explain the structure of the periodic table in terms of electrons — group number matches the number of outer-shell electrons (for main groups) and period number matches the number of occupied shells — and use this to predict similar properties within a group
826.ev: Links group number to outer-shell electrons for main-group elements
826.q: If {{name}} is told an unfamiliar element is in Group 2, Period 4, can they say how many outer electrons and shells it has, and which element it will behave like?

847.desc: Explain why simple molecular substances such as water, oxygen and methane have low melting and boiling points: the covalent bonds inside molecules are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak
847.ev: Distinguishes bonds within molecules from forces between molecules
847.q: If {{name}} is asked why water boils at only 100 °C when covalent bonds are strong, can they explain what actually gets overcome when water boils?

848.desc: Calculate the relative formula mass of a compound by adding the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in its formula
848.ev: Calculates Mr for compounds like CO₂ and Ca(OH)₂
848.q: If {{name}} is told carbon has relative atomic mass 12 and oxygen 16, can they work out the relative formula mass of carbon dioxide?

849.desc: Add state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) to equations and use them to tell, for example, which product is a gas that escapes or a precipitate that forms
849.ev: Adds correct state symbols to a balanced equation
849.q: If {{name}} sees CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), can they say which product bubbles out of the beaker?

850.desc: Explain how sulfur impurities in fuels form sulfur dioxide, how high engine temperatures form nitrogen oxides from air, and how particulates arise, describe their effects (acid rain, breathing problems, global dimming) and how they can be reduced
850.ev: Explains why sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form even though fuels are hydrocarbons
850.q: If {{name}} is asked why diesel cars are linked to poor city air, can they explain which pollutants form in the engine and why?

851.desc: Use bromine water to distinguish alkenes from alkanes: orange bromine water turns colourless with an alkene because bromine adds across the double bond
851.ev: Describes the result for an alkane and an alkene
851.q: If {{name}} has two unlabelled gases, propane and propene, can they describe a test to tell them apart?

852.desc: Explain absolute zero (0 K, about −273 °C) as the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy, and convert between degrees Celsius and kelvin
852.ev: Converts temperatures between °C and K by adding or subtracting 273
852.q: If {{name}} is told that liquid nitrogen boils at about 77 K, can they convert that to degrees Celsius and explain what 0 K would mean for the particles?

842.desc: Describe and explain how boiling point, viscosity and flammability of alkanes change with chain length, in terms of the strength of forces between molecules
842.ev: Describes the boiling point trend with chain length
842.q: If {{name}} compares petrol and candle wax, can they explain why the longer molecules in wax are solid and harder to light?

844.desc: Explain that carbon has four outer electrons and so forms four covalent bonds, and that carbon atoms can bond to each other in chains, branches and rings, giving millions of different compounds
844.ev: States that carbon forms four covalent bonds and links this to its four outer electrons
844.q: If {{name}} is told there are millions of known carbon compounds but only a few hundred of neon, can they explain the difference using outer electrons and bonding?

853.desc: Work out the formula of an ionic compound by balancing the charges on its ions, including compound ions such as sulfate, nitrate and hydroxide
853.ev: Writes formulae such as MgCl₂ and Al₂O₃ from ion charges
853.q: If {{name}} knows calcium forms Ca²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, can they work out the formula of calcium chloride and explain why?

854.desc: Explain acids as sources of H⁺ ions and alkalis as sources of OH⁻ ions in solution, write the ionic equation for neutralisation, and understand that each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration
854.ev: Writes H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O for neutralisation
854.q: If {{name}} compares lemon juice at pH 2 with vinegar at pH 3, can they say how many times more hydrogen ions the lemon juice has?

856.desc: Explain how many alkene monomers join to form an addition polymer, draw the repeating unit from the monomer and the monomer from the repeating unit, and name polymers such as poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene)
856.ev: Draws the repeating unit of poly(propene)
856.q: If {{name}} is shown a section of a polymer chain, can they draw the monomer it was made from?

855.desc: Describe how alkenes react by addition across the double bond with hydrogen (with a nickel catalyst), water (steam with a catalyst) and halogens, and draw the products
855.ev: Draws the product of ethene with bromine
855.q: If {{name}} sees ethene react with steam, can they draw the product and explain why it is called an addition reaction?

858.desc: Recognise alcohols by the –OH group, name and draw methanol to butanol, and describe their properties and uses as fuels and solvents
858.q: If {{name}} is told hand sanitiser contains an alcohol, can they draw ethanol and describe two of its properties?

861.desc: Describe alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (fast electrons from the nucleus) and gamma rays (electromagnetic waves), comparing their penetrating power, ionising power and range
861.ev: Identifies what each type of radiation is
861.q: If {{name}} is told a radiation source is stopped by a sheet of paper, can they identify which type it is and explain why it would still be dangerous if swallowed?

864.desc: Evaluate claims that biofuels such as bioethanol are carbon-neutral, using the carbon cycle and accounting for energy used in farming, processing and transport
864.ev: Explains why burning bioethanol is described as carbon-neutral
864.q: If {{name}} reads that biofuels are 'carbon-neutral', can they explain the reasoning and why the claim is only partly true?

865.desc: Explain that breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases energy, so whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on the balance of total bond energies
865.ev: States that bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic
865.q: If {{name}} is asked where the energy of burning methane comes from, can they explain it in terms of bonds broken and bonds made?

867.desc: Use a balanced equation and moles to calculate the mass of product formed or reactant needed, showing that atoms and mass are conserved mathematically
867.ev: Uses mole ratios from a balanced equation
867.q: If {{name}} burns 12 g of carbon completely, can they use C + O₂ → CO₂ to work out the mass of carbon dioxide made?

868.desc: Recognise carboxylic acids by the –COOH group, name methanoic to butanoic acid, describe their reactions with carbonates and metals, and explain that they are weak acids because they only partly ionise
868.q: If {{name}} adds vinegar to baking soda, can they name the gas produced and explain why vinegar is a weak acid?

870.desc: Measure and compare the energy released by burning alcohol fuels using simple calorimetry, and explain the trend with chain length in terms of bonds broken and made
870.ev: Calculates energy transferred using mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change
870.q: If {{name}} burns methanol and butanol to heat water, can they calculate which releases more energy per gram and explain why?

871.desc: Calculate the concentration of a solution in g/dm³ and mol/dm³, and explain how dilution changes concentration but not the amount of solute
871.ev: Calculates concentration from mass or moles and volume
871.q: If {{name}} dissolves 20 g of salt in 500 cm³ of water, can they work out the concentration in grams per dm³?

873.desc: Explain that condensation polymers form from monomers with two functional groups, losing a small molecule such as water at each link, and describe polyesters and polyamides
873.q: If {{name}} is given a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, can they show how a polyester forms and what is given off?

875.desc: Explain electrolysis as using electricity to break down a molten or dissolved ionic compound, predicting which ions move to each electrode and what forms there
875.ev: Explains why the compound must be molten or dissolved
875.q: If {{name}} passes electricity through molten lead bromide, can they predict what appears at each electrode and explain why?

872.desc: Describe how an alcohol and a carboxylic acid react with an acid catalyst to form an ester and water, name simple esters such as ethyl ethanoate, and give uses in flavourings and perfumes
872.ev: Writes a word equation for making ethyl ethanoate
872.q: If {{name}} warms ethanol with ethanoic acid and a few drops of sulfuric acid, can they predict what forms and why it smells fruity?

877.desc: Explain how temperature, concentration (or gas pressure), surface area and catalysts change the rate of a reaction, in terms of the frequency and energy of collisions
877.ev: Predicts the effect of each factor on rate
877.q: If {{name}} drops a whole indigestion tablet and a crushed one into water, can they predict which fizzes away faster and explain why?

857.desc: Explain that a functional group is the atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic reactions, and recognise C=C, –OH, –COOH and –COO– in structures
857.ev: Identifies the functional group in a given structure
857.q: If {{name}} is shown the structures of ethanol, ethanoic acid and ethene, can they circle the functional group in each and name the family?

878.desc: Describe and use the relationships between pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed mass of gas — pressure × volume is constant at constant temperature (Boyle's law), and volume or pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature — explaining each with particle collisions
878.ev: Uses p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ to find a new pressure or volume
878.q: If {{name}} squeezes a sealed syringe of air to half its volume, can they predict what happens to the pressure and explain it in terms of the particles?
