879.desc: Explain the properties of giant covalent structures — diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide — in terms of networks of strong covalent bonds, including why graphite conducts and is soft while diamond is hard
879.ev: Explains the very high melting points of giant covalent structures
879.q: If {{name}} is asked why pencil 'lead' (graphite) leaves marks on paper while diamond can cut glass — though both are pure carbon — can they explain using structure?

881.desc: Use bulk properties — melting and boiling point, conductivity, solubility, hardness — to infer the type of structure and strength of forces between particles in an unknown substance
881.ev: Classifies an unknown substance as ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent or metallic from data
881.q: If {{name}} is given a white solid that melts at 801 °C and conducts only when dissolved, can they decide what kind of structure it has and justify it?

882.desc: Describe the nucleus as protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force, which overcomes the electrical repulsion between protons at very short range, and recognise that some nuclei are unstable
882.ev: Explains why protons in a nucleus should repel each other
882.q: If {{name}} is asked why a nucleus full of positive protons doesn't fly apart, can they explain what holds it together?

862.desc: Compare making ethanol by fermenting sugars with yeast and by hydrating ethene with steam, weighing conditions, rate, purity, atom economy and use of renewable raw materials
862.q: If {{name}} is asked whether a country with lots of sugar cane but no oil should make ethanol by fermentation, can they justify their answer?

885.desc: Measure the rate of a reaction by tracking mass lost or gas produced over time, plot the results and use the gradient to compare rates, including the gradient of a tangent for an instantaneous rate
885.ev: Plans an experiment to collect gas volume over time
885.q: If {{name}} plots the volume of gas from a reaction every 10 seconds, can they use the graph to tell when the reaction was fastest and when it stopped?

880.desc: Explain metallic bonding as positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, and use it to explain conductivity, malleability and why alloys are harder than pure metals
880.ev: Draws and labels a model of metallic bonding
880.q: If {{name}} is asked why copper wire can be bent without snapping and also carries electricity, can they explain both using the structure of the metal?

886.desc: Explain how the molecular-level structure of designed materials — long-chain polymers, alloys, conducting metals, nanoparticles — determines how they function, and communicate this clearly
886.ev: Explains why polymers made of long tangled chains are flexible but strong
886.q: If {{name}} is asked why plastic bags stretch rather than snap, can they explain it in terms of the long molecules the plastic is made from?

887.desc: Name simple organic compounds using IUPAC stems (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-), suffixes (-ane, -ene, -ol, -oic acid) and position numbers, and draw a structure from its name
887.ev: Names a compound from its displayed formula
887.q: If {{name}} is given the name butan-1-ol, can they draw it and explain what each part of the name tells them?

889.desc: Describe proteins, starch, cellulose and DNA as natural condensation polymers built from amino acids, sugars and nucleotides
889.ev: Names the monomers of each natural polymer
889.q: If {{name}} learns that digestion breaks starch into glucose, can they explain this in terms of polymers and monomers?

890.desc: Describe how ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid by oxidising agents or by microbes in air, explaining why wine left open turns sour
890.ev: Writes a word equation for the oxidation of ethanol
890.q: If {{name}} leaves a bottle of wine open for a week, can they explain the chemistry behind it tasting sour?

892.desc: Evaluate ways of dealing with waste plastics (landfill, incineration, mechanical and chemical recycling, biodegradable polymers) using data on energy, emissions and persistence
892.ev: Explains why most addition polymers are not biodegradable
892.q: If {{name}} reads that a shopping bag is 'biodegradable', can they evaluate the claim and compare it with recycling a normal bag?

891.desc: Explain how chain length, branching and cross-linking affect polymer properties, and distinguish thermosoftening from thermosetting polymers in terms of forces and links between chains
891.q: If {{name}} compares a plastic bottle that softens in hot water with a saucepan handle that doesn't, can they explain the difference in structure?

893.desc: Predict and explain the products of simple reactions between main-group elements (e.g. sodium and chlorine, carbon and oxygen) using outer-electron arrangements and periodic trends
893.ev: Predicts the product and formula of a Group 1 metal reacting with a halogen
893.q: If {{name}} is asked what forms when potassium reacts with bromine, can they predict the product, write its formula and say why it forms?

859.desc: Explain that unstable nuclei decay randomly by emitting radiation — alpha and beta decay change the nucleus into a different element, while gamma emission releases energy without changing the numbers of protons and neutrons — and that we can predict how a large sample behaves but not when one nucleus will decay
859.q: If {{name}} is told a single atom of radon might decay in a second or in a week, can they explain how scientists can still predict what a big sample will do?

876.desc: Draw and interpret reaction profile diagrams showing the energy of reactants and products, the overall energy change and the activation energy, including the effect of a catalyst
876.ev: Draws profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions
876.q: If {{name}} is shown an energy diagram where the products are lower than the reactants, can they say whether the reaction heats or cools its surroundings and point out the activation energy?

894.desc: Calculate relative atomic mass as the weighted mean mass of an element's isotopes using their percentage abundances, and explain why values like chlorine's 35.5 are not whole numbers
894.ev: Calculates a weighted mean from isotope masses and abundances
894.q: If {{name}} learns that chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, can they show why its relative atomic mass is 35.5?

895.desc: Use the idea that changing state needs energy without a temperature change, and calculate the energy for a change of state using E = mL, distinguishing specific latent heat of fusion from vaporisation
895.ev: Explains that energy during a change of state breaks or weakens forces between particles rather than raising temperature
895.q: If {{name}} knows it takes 334 000 J to melt 1 kg of ice, can they work out the energy to melt a 0.2 kg ice cube and explain why the thermometer doesn't rise while it melts?

866.desc: Understand the mole as a fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10²³, the Avogadro constant), and convert between mass, moles and relative formula mass
866.ev: Uses moles = mass ÷ Mr in both directions
866.q: If {{name}} has 36 g of water (Mr 18), can they work out how many moles that is and roughly how many molecules?

898.desc: Recognise the polar C=O carbonyl group, with a δ+ carbon and δ− oxygen, in aldehydes (–CHO at the end of a chain) and ketones (C=O within the chain), and name them with -al and -one
898.ev: Distinguishes aldehydes from ketones by structure
898.q: If {{name}} is shown the structures of propanal and propanone, can they name each and explain how they differ?

901.desc: Explain that covalent bonds vibrate (stretch and bend) at frequencies in the infrared range that depend on bond strength and the masses of the atoms, so each bond absorbs infrared at characteristic frequencies
901.ev: Explains why bonds absorb infrared radiation
901.q: If {{name}} is asked why water vapour absorbs infrared radiation, can they explain in terms of bond vibrations?

903.desc: Classify organic reactions as combustion, addition, substitution, oxidation, condensation or cracking from equations, and choose a reaction to convert one compound into another
903.q: If {{name}} needs to turn ethene into ethyl ethanoate, can they plan a route and name each reaction type?

905.desc: Use curly arrows to show the movement of electron pairs in reaction mechanisms, such as electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene through a carbocation
905.ev: Explains what a curly arrow represents
905.q: If {{name}} is asked to show how HBr adds to ethene, can they draw a mechanism with correctly placed curly arrows?

908.desc: Explain why oxidising a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate and distilling off the product as it forms gives an aldehyde, while heating under reflux gives a carboxylic acid, and draw both set-ups
908.ev: Draws apparatus for distillation and for reflux
908.q: If {{name}} wants to make ethanal rather than ethanoic acid from ethanol, can they explain which apparatus to use and why?

910.desc: Explain that restricted rotation about a C=C bond can give E/Z (geometric) isomers when each carbon of the double bond has two different groups, and identify E and Z forms
910.ev: Explains why the C=C bond cannot rotate
910.q: If {{name}} draws but-2-ene in two ways, can they explain why these are different molecules but but-1-ene has no such pair?

912.desc: Describe electrons in s and p sub-shells and orbitals (an s orbital is spherical and a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, each holding two electrons), and write electron configurations such as 1s²2s²2p² for carbon
912.ev: Writes electron configurations for the first 20 elements using s and p notation
912.q: If {{name}} is asked for the electron configuration of carbon, can they write it using sub-shells and describe the orbitals involved?

913.desc: Calculate the empirical formula of a compound from masses or percentage composition by mass, dividing by relative atomic masses and finding the simplest whole-number ratio
913.ev: Calculates an empirical formula from percentages
913.q: If {{name}} knows a compound is 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass, can they find its empirical formula?

915.desc: Explain that esterification is reversible and reaches equilibrium, and suggest ways to increase the yield of ester such as using excess alcohol or removing water
915.ev: Writes the equilibrium equation for esterification
915.q: If {{name}} wants more ethyl ethanoate from a reaction mixture, can they suggest a change and explain it with Le Chatelier's principle?

746.desc: Define half-life as the time for half the unstable nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to decay, read half-life from a decay graph and calculate how much remains after a number of half-lives
746.ev: Reads half-life from an activity–time graph
746.q: If {{name}} is told a sample has a half-life of 6 hours, can they work out what fraction is left after a day?

916.desc: Name and draw haloalkanes, describe their uses and reactions in which the halogen is replaced, and explain why CFCs damage the ozone layer
916.ev: Names a haloalkane from its structure
916.q: If {{name}} is told CFCs were once used in fridges, can they draw one and explain why they were phased out?

918.desc: Describe the stages of a time-of-flight mass spectrometer (ionisation, acceleration, a flight tube where lighter ions travel faster, and detection) and explain that ions are separated by mass-to-charge ratio
918.ev: Describes each stage of the mass spectrometer
918.q: If {{name}} is shown a diagram of a time-of-flight mass spectrometer, can they explain how it separates ions?

919.desc: Explain chromatography in terms of a stationary phase and a mobile phase, with substances separating because they are attracted to the two phases to different extents
919.ev: Identifies the stationary and mobile phases in paper chromatography
919.q: If {{name}} sees ink split into three spots, can they explain why the dyes moved different distances?

921.desc: Explain why chemists use instrumental methods (mass spectrometry, infrared and NMR spectroscopy) alongside chemical tests: they are fast, sensitive, need small samples and give different, complementary information about structure
921.ev: Compares instrumental methods with chemical tests
921.q: If {{name}} is identifying an unknown liquid, can they explain what instrumental methods add to chemical tests?

923.desc: Use a data table of characteristic absorptions to identify functional groups, such as a broad O–H in alcohols (about 3200–3550 cm⁻¹), a very broad O–H in carboxylic acids (about 2500–3300 cm⁻¹) and a strong C=O (about 1680–1750 cm⁻¹)
923.ev: Identifies an alcohol, an aldehyde or ketone, and a carboxylic acid from spectra
923.q: If {{name}} is given the IR spectrum of an unknown compound with a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad peak above 2500 cm⁻¹, can they identify the functional group?

924.desc: Explain how breathalysers and gas monitors detect substances such as ethanol, carbon monoxide or carbon dioxide by measuring the absorption of infrared at a characteristic wavenumber
924.ev: Explains how an IR breathalyser measures ethanol
924.q: If {{name}} is asked how a roadside breathalyser works, can they explain the role of infrared absorption?

897.desc: Distinguish London (induced dipole) forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds between N–H, O–H or F–H groups and lone pairs, and use them to explain trends in boiling point and solubility
897.ev: Identifies the strongest intermolecular force in a substance
897.q: If {{name}} compares ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) with propane (−42 °C), which have similar masses, can they explain the difference?

925.desc: Identify the limiting reactant in a mixture, explain why the other is in excess, and calculate theoretical and percentage yield
925.ev: Identifies the limiting reactant from given masses
925.q: If {{name}} makes sandwiches with 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese, can they use that idea to explain what a limiting reactant is in a chemical reaction?

926.desc: Read the mass spectrum of an element to find its isotopes and their relative abundances, calculate the relative atomic mass, and predict the peaks for a diatomic element such as Cl₂ (at 70, 72 and 74 in the ratio 9:6:1)
926.ev: Reads isotopic masses and abundances from a spectrum
926.q: If {{name}} is given the mass spectrum of a sample of magnesium, can they find its relative atomic mass?

928.desc: Find the molecular formula from the empirical formula and the relative molecular mass, such as one read from the molecular ion peak
928.ev: Finds the molecular formula from CH₂ and Mr = 56
928.q: If {{name}} has found an empirical formula of CH₂O and a molecular ion at 60, can they find the molecular formula?

929.desc: Write balanced nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay, showing that the total mass number and total atomic number are conserved even though the element changes
929.ev: Writes an alpha decay equation for a given nucleus
929.q: If {{name}} is told uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay, can they work out the mass number and atomic number of the nucleus it becomes?

931.desc: Explain nuclear fission as a large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei and releasing neutrons and energy, and how a controlled chain reaction is used in a nuclear power station
931.ev: Describes fission of uranium-235 after absorbing a neutron
931.q: If {{name}} is asked what control rods in a nuclear reactor are for, can they explain using the idea of a chain reaction?

933.desc: Explain nuclear fusion as light nuclei joining to make a heavier nucleus, releasing energy, why it needs extremely high temperature and pressure, and that it powers the Sun
933.ev: Describes hydrogen nuclei fusing to make helium
933.q: If {{name}} is asked how the Sun produces its energy, can they explain fusion and why it needs such a hot core?

934.desc: Define oxidation as loss of electrons and reduction as gain of electrons, identify what is oxidised and reduced in displacement reactions, and connect this to extracting metals
934.ev: Identifies oxidation and reduction in a displacement reaction
934.q: If {{name}} puts an iron nail in copper sulfate solution and it turns pink, can they explain which substance lost electrons and which gained them?

907.desc: Explain that aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass (permanent dipoles) but lower than alcohols (no hydrogen bonds between molecules), and that small ones dissolve in water by hydrogen bonding to it
907.ev: Orders an alkane, aldehyde and alcohol of similar Mr by boiling point
907.q: If {{name}} is given butane, propanal and propan-1-ol, can they put them in order of boiling point and explain the order?

906.desc: Classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary from their structure and predict their oxidation products: aldehydes then carboxylic acids, ketones, or no reaction
906.q: If {{name}} oxidises propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, can they predict different products and explain why?

935.desc: Distinguish irradiation from contamination, explain how dose, half-life and type of radiation affect risk, and evaluate uses of radiation in medicine and industry
935.q: If {{name}} is asked why a hospital tracer should have a short half-life, can they explain the trade-off between doing its job and keeping the patient safe?

922.desc: Read an infrared spectrum with transmittance against wavenumber (in cm⁻¹, from about 4000 down to 500), recognising absorptions as downward troughs and the fingerprint region below about 1500 cm⁻¹
922.q: If {{name}} is shown an infrared spectrum, can they read the wavenumber of the strongest absorption and explain the axes?

937.desc: Explain that some reactions are reversible and that in a closed system they reach dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates so amounts stay constant
937.q: If {{name}} sees blue copper sulfate turn white when heated and blue again when water is added, can they explain what makes this reaction reversible?

938.desc: Calculate Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent, and identify substances by comparing Rf values with known samples under the same conditions
938.ev: Calculates an Rf value from a chromatogram
938.q: If {{name}} has a spot 3.6 cm from the start and a solvent front at 9.0 cm, can they find the Rf value and use it to identify the substance?

939.desc: Predict the shapes and bond angles of simple molecules and ions from the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), pyramidal (107°) and bent (104.5°)
939.ev: Predicts the shape of CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O
939.q: If {{name}} is asked why the bond angle in water is smaller than in methane, can they explain using electron pairs?

914.desc: Predict how changing concentration, temperature or pressure shifts the position of an equilibrium, and use this to refine conditions that increase the yield of a product (e.g. in the Haber process)
914.ev: Predicts the direction of shift when a product is removed
914.q: If {{name}} is told a reaction that makes ammonia gives out heat, can they predict whether cooling it would give more or less ammonia, and why factories don't simply make it very cold?

896.desc: Explain that a σ bond forms by end-on overlap of orbitals and a π bond by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis, so a C=C double bond is one σ and one π bond and cannot rotate
896.ev: Describes how σ and π bonds form
896.q: If {{name}} is shown the double bond in ethene, can they describe it in terms of σ and π bonds and explain why it is a site of reactivity?

904.desc: Read and draw skeletal formulae, where lines represent carbon chains and hydrogens on carbon are implied, and convert to and from displayed formulae
904.ev: Draws the skeletal formula of pentane
904.q: If {{name}} sees a zig-zag line with an OH at the end, can they name the molecule and give its molecular formula?

899.desc: Explain that different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum probe different changes in molecules (radio waves for nuclear spin in NMR, infrared for bond vibrations, visible and ultraviolet for electron transitions), because the photon energy must match the energy change
899.ev: Matches each spectroscopic technique to its region of the spectrum
899.q: If {{name}} is asked why NMR uses radio waves but IR spectroscopy uses infrared, can they explain using photon energy?

909.desc: Explain that structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures (chain, position or functional-group isomers), and draw and name isomers of small molecules
909.q: If {{name}} is told butane and methylpropane are both C₄H₁₀, can they draw both and explain why they are different compounds?

902.desc: Describe how alkanes react with halogens in UV light by substitution, replacing hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms, and explain why mixtures of products form
902.ev: Writes an equation for methane with chlorine
902.q: If {{name}} mixes methane and chlorine in sunlight, can they predict a product and explain why the reaction is called substitution?

920.desc: Use chemical tests to identify functional groups: bromine water for C=C, sodium carbonate for –COOH, and acidified potassium dichromate for primary and secondary alcohols
920.ev: States the positive result for each test
920.q: If {{name}} has three unlabelled liquids, an alkene, an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, can they plan tests to identify each?

943.desc: Draw and describe Kekulé's model of benzene as a six-membered carbon ring with alternating single and double bonds, and the delocalised ring symbol used today
943.ev: Draws the Kekulé structure with displayed and skeletal formulae
943.q: If {{name}} draws the Kekulé structure of benzene, can they say what it predicts about the carbon–carbon bond lengths?

927.desc: Identify the molecular ion peak (M⁺) in the mass spectrum of a compound as the peak with the highest m/z, apart from small isotope peaks, and use it to find the relative molecular mass
927.q: If {{name}} is shown the mass spectrum of an unknown hydrocarbon, can they find its relative molecular mass?

942.desc: Explain that benzene, C₆H₆, appears highly unsaturated from its formula yet does not readily undergo addition reactions or decolourise bromine water, which a structure must explain
942.ev: Calculates that C₆H₆ has far fewer hydrogens than hexane
942.q: If {{name}} compares benzene with cyclohexene, can they explain why benzene's formula and its reactions seem to contradict each other?

944.desc: Compare the energy released in nuclear processes with chemical reactions — millions of times more per kilogram — and explain qualitatively that the energy comes from a tiny decrease in mass (E = mc²)
944.ev: States that nuclear reactions release far more energy per kg than burning fuel
944.q: If {{name}} hears that a small pellet of nuclear fuel releases as much energy as a tonne of coal, can they explain where that enormous energy comes from?

911.desc: Describe and explain trends in atomic radius and in how easily atoms lose electrons across a period and down a group, using nuclear charge and shielding qualitatively
911.ev: States that atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group
911.q: If {{name}} compares sodium and chlorine in the same row of the periodic table, can they explain why chlorine's atoms are smaller even though they have more electrons?

947.desc: Describe acid anhydrides reacting like acyl chlorides but more slowly, and explain why ethanoic anhydride is preferred industrially, for example in making aspirin from 2-hydroxybenzoic acid
947.ev: Writes the equation for ethanoic anhydride with an alcohol
947.q: If {{name}} is asked why aspirin is made with ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride, can they give at least two reasons?

949.desc: Describe the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with KCN followed by dilute acid to form hydroxynitriles, explain the mechanism, and recognise it as a way to add a carbon atom to a chain
949.ev: Writes the equation and names the hydroxynitrile
949.q: If {{name}} reacts ethanal with KCN and acid, can they draw the product and explain how its carbon chain has changed?

951.desc: Recognise primary and N-substituted amides, describe their formation from acyl chlorides with ammonia or amines, and identify the amide link in polyamides and proteins
951.ev: Draws ethanamide and an N-substituted amide
951.q: If {{name}} reacts ethanoyl chloride with methylamine, can they draw and name the product?

950.desc: Classify amines as primary, secondary or tertiary, explain their basicity using the nitrogen lone pair, and describe making amines from haloalkanes and ammonia, including why mixtures form
950.q: If {{name}} reacts bromoethane with ammonia, can they explain why several amine products form and how to favour ethylamine?

955.desc: Explain that amino acids react with both acids and bases: in acidic solution the amine group gains H⁺ (–NH₃⁺) and in alkaline solution the carboxylic acid group loses H⁺ (–COO⁻)
955.ev: Draws the form of glycine in acid
955.q: If {{name}} adds hydrochloric acid to glycine, can they draw the ion formed?

953.desc: Describe phenylamine as a base that accepts H⁺ using the nitrogen lone pair, and explain why it is a weaker base than ammonia because the lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring
953.ev: Writes the equation for phenylamine and hydrochloric acid
953.q: If {{name}} is asked whether phenylamine or ammonia is the stronger base, can they explain their answer?

960.desc: Interpret ¹³C NMR spectra, using the number of peaks for the number of carbon environments and shift ranges (such as C=O at about 160–220 ppm) to identify groups, knowing that routine spectra show single peaks whose heights are not proportional to the number of carbons
960.ev: Counts carbon environments from a spectrum
960.q: If {{name}} is given the ¹³C NMR spectrum of a C₄H₈O compound with four peaks, one at 209 ppm, can they suggest a structure?

961.desc: Recognise esters, acyl chlorides, acid anhydrides and amides as derivatives of carboxylic acids in which the –OH is replaced, and compare their reactivity
961.ev: Draws and names one example of each derivative
961.q: If {{name}} is shown ethanoyl chloride, ethanoic anhydride, ethyl ethanoate and ethanamide, can they explain how each is related to ethanoic acid?

959.desc: Use symmetry to decide how many different chemical environments of carbon or hydrogen atoms a molecule has, such as two carbon environments and three hydrogen environments in propan-2-ol
959.ev: Counts carbon environments in a molecule
959.q: If {{name}} compares propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, can they predict how many carbon environments each has?

958.desc: Use chemical shift (δ, in ppm relative to TMS) and data tables to identify environments, explaining that nearby electronegative atoms such as oxygen move absorptions to higher δ
958.ev: Assigns peaks to environments using a data table
958.q: If {{name}} sees a ¹H NMR peak at δ = 3.6, can they use a data table to suggest the environment?

963.desc: Identify a chiral carbon as one bonded to four different groups, and explain that such a molecule has two non-superimposable mirror-image forms called enantiomers
963.ev: Marks the chiral carbon in a structure
963.q: If {{name}} is given butan-2-ol, can they find the chiral carbon and draw both enantiomers in 3-D?

964.desc: Explain that every α-amino acid except glycine has a chiral carbon, and that the amino acids in natural proteins are almost all one enantiomer (the L form)
964.ev: Explains why glycine is not chiral
964.q: If {{name}} compares glycine and alanine, can they explain why only alanine has optical isomers?

968.desc: Choose between paper, thin-layer, column and gas chromatography for a task, comparing Rf values with retention times and identification with purification
968.ev: Matches a task to a suitable method
968.q: If {{name}} needs to identify traces of a pesticide in fruit, can they choose a chromatography method and explain why?

966.desc: Use column chromatography to separate and collect the components of a mixture, choosing the solvent and collecting fractions
966.ev: Describes how a column is packed and run
966.q: If {{name}} needs to purify a reaction product from a by-product, can they explain how column chromatography would do it?

972.desc: Deduce the structure of an unknown organic compound by combining evidence from percentage composition, mass spectrometry, infrared, ¹³C NMR and ¹H NMR spectra and checking that every piece of evidence agrees
972.ev: Uses each technique for the information it gives best
972.q: If {{name}} is given the composition, mass spectrum, IR spectrum and both NMR spectra of an unknown compound, can they deduce its structure and justify it?

975.desc: Describe coupling a diazonium salt with a phenol in alkaline solution to form an azo compound containing –N=N– linking two rings, and explain the use of azo compounds as dyes
975.ev: Writes the coupling reaction with phenol
975.q: If {{name}} mixes benzenediazonium chloride with alkaline phenol, can they draw the coloured product?

976.desc: Use 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent), which gives a yellow-orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones, and identify the compound from the melting point of the purified derivative
976.q: If {{name}} gets an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP, can they explain what this shows and how to identify the exact compound?

973.desc: Describe making benzenediazonium chloride from phenylamine with nitrous acid (sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid) below 10 °C, and explain why the salt must be kept cold
973.q: If {{name}} is preparing a diazonium salt, can they explain why the mixture is kept in an ice bath?

980.desc: Use the directing effects of substituents to predict products: –OH, –NH₂ and –CH₃ activate the ring and direct to the 2- and 4-positions, while –NO₂ deactivates the ring and directs to the 3-position
980.ev: Predicts the product of nitrating methylbenzene
980.q: If {{name}} needs to make 3-bromonitrobenzene from benzene, can they decide which substituent to add first?

981.desc: Explain that an electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to regions of high electron density, such as the delocalised ring of benzene, and identify electrophiles such as NO₂⁺ and polarised halogens
981.q: If {{name}} is given a list of species, can they pick out the electrophiles and explain why benzene reacts with them?

974.desc: Draw the general mechanism of electrophilic substitution: the electrophile accepts a pair of electrons from the ring to form a positively charged intermediate that has lost its delocalisation, and loss of H⁺ restores the ring
974.ev: Draws the curly arrows for each step
974.q: If {{name}} is given a benzene ring and an electrophile E⁺, can they draw the mechanism of substitution?

983.desc: Compare benzene's enthalpy of hydrogenation (about −208 kJ mol⁻¹) with the value predicted for the Kekulé structure (three times cyclohexene's −120 kJ mol⁻¹, about −360 kJ mol⁻¹), and show the extra stability on an energy diagram
983.ev: Calculates the expected enthalpy of hydrogenation for the Kekulé structure
983.q: If {{name}} is given the enthalpies of hydrogenation of cyclohexene and benzene, can they use them to argue that benzene is more stable than the Kekulé model predicts?

986.desc: Explain enzymes as protein catalysts whose active site matches a substrate in shape (and often in chirality), and how heat or a change in pH denatures them by disrupting hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions
986.ev: Explains specificity in terms of the active site
986.q: If {{name}} sees that an enzyme stops working at 70 °C, can they explain what has happened to its structure?

987.desc: Evaluate the evidence that led chemists to modify the Kekulé model: all six C–C bonds have the same length (0.139 nm, between C–C at 0.154 nm and C=C at 0.134 nm), the enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than predicted, and benzene resists addition
987.ev: States the bond-length evidence from X-ray diffraction
987.q: If {{name}} is asked why chemists no longer accept the Kekulé structure, can they give three pieces of evidence?

990.desc: Explain why reactions that make new C–C bonds matter in synthesis, and compare the methods available: cyanide addition or substitution followed by nitrile reactions, and Friedel–Crafts reactions on aromatic rings
990.ev: Lists reactions that form new C–C bonds
990.q: If {{name}} needs a product with one more carbon than the starting material, can they choose a reaction that forms a new C–C bond?

970.desc: Explain that molecular ions break into a positive fragment ion and a neutral radical, identify common fragments (such as CH₃⁺ at 15, C₂H₅⁺ at 29, CH₃CO⁺ at 43 and C₆H₅⁺ at 77) and use them to distinguish isomers
970.ev: Writes an equation for a fragmentation
970.q: If {{name}} sees a large peak at m/z = 43 in the spectrum of a ketone, can they suggest which fragment causes it?

988.desc: Describe Friedel–Crafts acylation (an acyl chloride with an AlCl₃ catalyst forming an aromatic ketone) and alkylation as ways to form new C–C bonds to a benzene ring
988.ev: Writes the equation for acylation of benzene
988.q: If {{name}} needs to make phenylethanone from benzene, can they give the reagents and catalyst?

993.desc: Explain that magnetic resonance imaging uses the same principle as NMR, detecting hydrogen nuclei in water and fat in the body with radio waves in a strong magnetic field, and compare its risks with X-ray imaging
993.q: If {{name}} is asked why an MRI scan does not carry the same risks as a CT scan, can they explain?

995.desc: Build and use a map of conversions between alkanes, alkenes, haloalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, acyl chlorides, amides, amines and nitriles, with reagents and conditions for each step
995.ev: Draws a reaction map with reagents on each arrow
995.q: If {{name}} is asked how to turn propan-1-ol into propanamide, can they use a reaction map to find a route?

967.desc: Explain how gas chromatography separates a mixture by retention time and mass spectrometry then identifies each component, with uses in forensics, drug testing and environmental monitoring
967.q: If {{name}} is asked how a laboratory identifies a banned substance in an athlete's urine, can they explain GC–MS?

991.desc: Describe the bromination or chlorination of benzene using a halogen carrier (such as FeBr₃ for bromine or AlCl₃ for chlorine), which polarises the halogen to generate the electrophile, and contrast it with addition to alkenes
991.q: If {{name}} is asked why benzene needs a catalyst to react with bromine when cyclohexene does not, can they explain?

996.desc: Use accurate masses to four decimal places to decide between molecular formulae with the same nominal mass, such as CO (27.9949), N₂ (28.0061) and C₂H₄ (28.0313)
996.ev: Calculates accurate masses from isotopic masses
996.q: If {{name}} is told a compound has M⁺ at 44.0262, can they decide between C₂H₄O, CO₂ and C₃H₈?

962.desc: Explain that nuclei such as ¹H and ¹³C behave like tiny magnets, so in a strong magnetic field they absorb radio-frequency radiation at frequencies that depend on their chemical environment, measured relative to TMS
962.ev: Explains why a strong magnetic field is needed
962.q: If {{name}} is asked what is actually absorbed in an NMR spectrometer, can they explain in terms of nuclei, a magnetic field and radio waves?

998.desc: Compare acid hydrolysis of esters (reversible, giving a carboxylic acid and an alcohol) with alkaline hydrolysis (irreversible, giving a carboxylate salt), and apply alkaline hydrolysis of fats to soap making
998.ev: Writes equations for acid and alkaline hydrolysis of an ester
998.q: If {{name}} heats ethyl ethanoate with sodium hydroxide, can they name the products and explain why the reaction does not reverse?

1000.desc: Describe the hydrolysis of peptides and proteins to amino acids by heating with concentrated hydrochloric acid or by enzymes, and predict the products
1000.ev: Writes the products of hydrolysing a dipeptide
1000.q: If {{name}} hydrolyses a tripeptide, can they draw the amino acids produced?

1003.desc: Identify O–H and N–H peaks in ¹H NMR spectra by shaking the sample with D₂O, which exchanges these protons for deuterium so their peaks disappear, and recognise that O–H peaks are usually singlets
1003.ev: Explains why the O–H peak disappears with D₂O
1003.q: If {{name}} sees a peak vanish after adding D₂O, can they explain what it tells them about the molecule?

1005.desc: Identify an unknown carbonyl compound by combining 2,4-DNP, Tollens' or Fehling's results, the melting point of a derivative, and IR and NMR evidence such as the aldehyde proton near δ 9–10
1005.q: If {{name}} is given test results and spectra for a C₄H₈O compound, can they decide whether it is butanal or butanone?

971.desc: Combine chemical shift, integration and splitting from a ¹H NMR spectrum to deduce the structure of a compound with a known molecular formula
971.ev: Assigns every peak in a spectrum
971.q: If {{name}} is given the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ and a ¹H NMR spectrum, can they deduce which ester it is?

1006.desc: Use the small M+1 peak (from carbon-13, about 1.1% per carbon atom) to estimate the number of carbon atoms, and M+2 peaks to detect chlorine (M:M+2 about 3:1) or bromine (about 1:1)
1006.ev: Estimates the number of carbons from the M+1 peak
1006.q: If {{name}} sees two molecular-ion peaks of equal height two mass units apart, can they explain what element the compound contains?

956.desc: Describe the reduction of nitrobenzene to phenylamine using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid followed by sodium hydroxide
956.ev: States the reagents for the reduction
956.q: If {{name}} has made nitrobenzene, can they explain how to turn it into phenylamine?

979.desc: Name simple aromatic compounds (methylbenzene, chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, phenol, benzoic acid, phenylamine) and number the ring for disubstituted compounds
979.q: If {{name}} is shown benzene rings with –NO₂, –OH and –CH₃ groups, can they name each compound?

978.desc: Describe the nitration of benzene with concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids at no more than about 50 °C, including the formation of the NO₂⁺ electrophile (HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻)
978.q: If {{name}} is asked how nitrobenzene is made, can they give the reagents, conditions and the electrophile?

989.desc: Describe hydrolysing nitriles to carboxylic acids and reducing them to primary amines, and use these reactions after adding cyanide to extend a carbon chain
989.ev: Writes the equation for hydrolysis of a nitrile
989.q: If {{name}} needs to convert ethanal into 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, can they plan the steps?

952.desc: Explain that a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor that attacks a δ+ atom, identify nucleophiles such as OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and the hydride ion from NaBH₄, and contrast them with electrophiles
952.q: If {{name}} is given OH⁻, NO₂⁺, NH₃ and Br₂, can they sort them into nucleophiles and electrophiles and explain why?

948.desc: Draw the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to C=O: the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon, the π electrons move onto oxygen, and the intermediate is protonated
948.ev: Draws curly arrows for each step
948.q: If {{name}} is given propanal and the CN⁻ ion, can they draw the mechanism of the reaction?

1007.desc: Draw the addition–elimination mechanism for an acyl chloride with a nucleophile such as water, an alcohol or ammonia, showing addition to C=O, reformation of C=O and loss of Cl⁻ and H⁺
1007.ev: Draws the mechanism for ethanoyl chloride and methanol
1007.q: If {{name}} is given ethanoyl chloride and ammonia, can they draw the full mechanism?

1009.desc: Explain that enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions, that a racemic mixture gives no overall rotation, and how a polarimeter measures this
1009.ev: Describes the effect of each enantiomer on plane-polarised light
1009.q: If {{name}} finds that a sample has no effect on plane-polarised light, can they give two possible explanations?

969.desc: Use the main organic preparation and purification techniques: heating under reflux, distillation, separating funnel, drying with an anhydrous salt, recrystallisation, and melting-point determination
969.ev: Explains when to use reflux and when to distil
969.q: If {{name}} has made an impure solid product, can they describe how to purify it and check its purity?

1011.desc: Calculate the overall yield of a multi-step synthesis by multiplying the yields of each step, and compare routes using atom economy and the number of steps
1011.ev: Calculates the overall yield of a three-step route
1011.q: If {{name}} has a three-step route with yields of 80%, 70% and 90%, can they find the overall yield and suggest how to improve it?

999.desc: Show how two amino acids join by a condensation reaction to form a dipeptide with a peptide (amide) link, and work out the two possible dipeptides from two different amino acids
999.ev: Draws the dipeptide formed from glycine and alanine
999.q: If {{name}} is given glycine and alanine, can they draw both dipeptides they can form?

946.desc: Describe phenols as compounds with –OH bonded directly to a benzene ring, explain that phenol is a weak acid that reacts with sodium hydroxide but not sodium carbonate, and distinguish it from alcohols and carboxylic acids
946.ev: Identifies phenols and distinguishes them from alcohols
946.q: If {{name}} has unlabelled samples of ethanol, phenol and ethanoic acid, can they plan tests to identify each?

1010.desc: Plan two- to four-step syntheses by working back from the target (retrosynthesis), choosing reagents and conditions, and judging routes by number of steps, yield, safety and cost
1010.ev: Works backwards from a target to a starting material
1010.q: If {{name}} needs to make propanoic acid from ethene, can they plan a route that adds the extra carbon?

1012.desc: Plan two- or three-step syntheses of aromatic compounds, such as benzene to nitrobenzene to phenylamine to an azo dye, giving reagents and conditions and considering directing effects
1012.ev: Plans a route from benzene to an azo dye
1012.q: If {{name}} needs to make a dye from benzene, can they plan the route with reagents and conditions?

1013.desc: Draw repeat units of polyesters and polyamides made from diols, diamines and dicarboxylic acids or diacyl chlorides (such as PET and nylon-6,6), and explain their hydrolysis by acids and alkalis and their biodegradability
1013.ev: Draws the repeat unit from a diamine and a diacyl chloride
1013.q: If {{name}} is given a section of nylon-6,6, can they identify the monomers and explain how it could be broken down?

984.desc: Describe protein structure as the amino-acid sequence (primary), α-helices and β-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds (secondary), and the 3-D fold held by hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions (tertiary)
984.ev: Describes each level of protein structure
984.q: If {{name}} is asked how a single chain of amino acids folds into a specific shape, can they name the interactions that hold it?

1015.desc: Compare proteins with synthetic polyamides such as nylon: both have amide links, but proteins have many different R groups in a specific sequence that gives them a precise folded shape
1015.ev: Identifies the amide links in nylon and in a protein
1015.q: If {{name}} compares a section of nylon-6,6 with a section of a protein, can they describe one similarity and two differences?

1001.desc: Use the relative areas of ¹H NMR peaks, often shown as an integration trace, to find the ratio of hydrogen atoms in each environment
1001.ev: Finds the ratio of hydrogens from integration values
1001.q: If {{name}} sees ¹H NMR peaks with areas in the ratio 3:2:1, can they suggest which groups of hydrogens they represent?

1016.desc: Explain that nucleophilic attack on a planar C=O group is equally likely from either side, giving a racemic mixture, and why medicines often need a single enantiomer (as the thalidomide case showed)
1016.ev: Explains why adding HCN to ethanal gives a racemic product
1016.q: If {{name}} makes 2-hydroxypropanenitrile from ethanal, can they explain why the product is optically inactive?

945.desc: Describe the vigorous reactions of acyl chlorides with water (carboxylic acid), alcohols (esters), ammonia (amides) and amines (N-substituted amides), each releasing HCl, and explain why they are better than carboxylic acids for making esters
945.ev: Writes equations for ethanoyl chloride with water, ethanol and ammonia
945.q: If {{name}} needs to make ethyl ethanoate in high yield, can they explain why ethanoyl chloride works better than ethanoic acid?

994.desc: Reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols with NaBH₄, writing equations with [H], and recognise this as the reverse of oxidation
994.ev: Writes the equation for the reduction of propanone using [H]
994.q: If {{name}} reduces butanal and butanone with NaBH₄, can they name both products and classify them?

1018.desc: Explain how amino acids carry different charges at a given pH and so move differently in an electric field (electrophoresis), with no movement at the isoelectric point
1018.ev: Predicts the charge of an amino acid above and below its isoelectric point
1018.q: If {{name}} runs electrophoresis of glycine at pH 2, can they predict which electrode it moves towards?

1002.desc: Use the n + 1 rule (a peak is split into n + 1 lines by n hydrogens on adjacent carbons) to identify singlets, doublets, triplets and quartets, recognising patterns such as the ethyl group's triplet and quartet
1002.ev: Predicts the splitting for each environment
1002.q: If {{name}} sees a triplet and a quartet in a ¹H NMR spectrum, can they explain which group is likely to be present?

954.desc: Recognise α-amino acids as H₂N–CHR–COOH, with an amine group and a carboxylic acid group on the same carbon and a side chain R that differs between amino acids
954.ev: Draws the general structure of an amino acid
954.q: If {{name}} is shown the structure of alanine, can they identify the amine, carboxylic acid and R groups?

957.desc: Describe benzene as a planar ring of six carbon atoms with 120° bond angles in which one p orbital from each carbon overlaps sideways to form a ring of six delocalised π electrons above and below the plane
957.ev: Describes the overlap of p orbitals in benzene
957.q: If {{name}} is asked to explain why all the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are the same length, can they use the delocalised model?

965.desc: Use thin-layer chromatography to identify the amino acids in a hydrolysed protein, locating colourless spots with ninhydrin or UV light and comparing Rf values with standards
965.ev: Describes how to run a TLC plate
965.q: If {{name}} hydrolyses a peptide and runs TLC, can they explain how to find which amino acids it contained?

1004.desc: Use Tollens' reagent (a silver mirror forms) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (blue to brick-red precipitate) to distinguish aldehydes, which are easily oxidised, from ketones, which are not
1004.ev: States the positive results for both tests
1004.q: If {{name}} has two unlabelled colourless liquids, propanal and propanone, can they choose a test to tell them apart and predict the results?

1019.desc: Use IR spectra to show that a reaction has happened, such as the oxidation of an alcohol (O–H absorption disappears, C=O appears), and compare fingerprint regions with reference spectra to identify a product
1019.ev: Explains how IR shows an alcohol has been oxidised
1019.q: If {{name}} has oxidised propan-2-ol, can they explain how an IR spectrum would show the reaction worked?

982.desc: Explain that addition to benzene would disrupt the delocalised ring and lose its extra stability, whereas substitution replaces a hydrogen and keeps the ring intact
982.ev: Explains why addition is energetically unfavourable for benzene
982.q: If {{name}} sees that bromine adds to cyclohexene but substitutes into benzene, can they explain the difference?

1021.desc: Explain that extended delocalised systems such as azo dyes absorb visible light because the energy gap for electron transitions is smaller, so the compound appears the complementary colour
1021.ev: Links absorbed wavelengths to the colour seen
1021.q: If {{name}} is shown a yellow azo dye, can they explain which light it absorbs and why?

977.desc: Explain that a lone pair on the oxygen of phenol is partly delocalised into the ring, increasing its electron density, so phenol decolourises bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst to form a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
977.ev: Describes the reaction of phenol with bromine water
977.q: If {{name}} sees phenol instantly decolourise bromine water, can they explain why benzene does not?

1014.desc: Explain that amino acids exist as zwitterions (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻) at their isoelectric point, and use this to explain their high melting points and solubility in water
1014.ev: Draws the zwitterion of an amino acid
1014.q: If {{name}} is told glycine melts at over 200 °C while ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C, can they explain the difference?

probes.q: If {{name}} was pushing a heavy box along the floor but it wasn't moving, could they explain all the forces acting on it and why it stays still even though you're pushing?
If {{name}} is told a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds, can they work out its acceleration and explain what the number means?
If {{name}} rolls a ball off a 1.25 m high table at 2 m/s, can they work out how far from the table it lands?

1043.desc: Draw and interpret force diagrams showing forces as labelled arrows — where the arrow's length represents the force's magnitude and its direction shows which way the force acts; show multiple forces on one object; identify from the diagram whether forces are balanced (equal arrows in opposite directions, no resultant) or unbalanced (arrows of different sizes, producing a resultant); represent the resultant with a single arrow
1043.ev: Draw a force diagram with labelled arrows showing direction and relative size for at least two forces acting on an object
1043.q: If {{name}} is asked to draw a diagram of all the forces acting on a stationary book on a table, can they draw two arrows — one pointing down for gravity and one pointing up from the table — and explain why, if they're balanced, the book doesn't move?

57.desc: Read and plot distance-time graphs for moving objects; interpret the gradient (steepness) of a line as speed; identify stationary periods (horizontal sections), constant speed (straight diagonal lines), and relative speeds by comparing gradients; calculate average speed from the gradient of a straight-line segment using speed = distance ÷ time
57.ev: Read a distance-time graph and describe what is happening at each stage — moving, stopped, returning
57.q: If {{name}} sees a distance-time graph of a journey with a flat section in the middle, can they explain what was happening then — and point to which part of the graph shows the fastest speed?

874.desc: Understand that electric current is the rate of flow of charge (measured in amperes using an ammeter), and that potential difference (voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge (measured in volts using a voltmeter)
874.ev: States that current is measured in amperes (A) and is the rate at which charge flows around a circuit
874.q: If {{name}} sets up a circuit with an ammeter and a voltmeter, can they explain what each one is measuring and describe the difference between current and voltage?

807.desc: Explain the principle of conservation of energy (energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores), and describe how energy is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings in all real processes
807.ev: States the law of conservation of energy
807.q: If {{name}} charged their phone overnight and was asked where the electrical energy goes, could they explain what conservation of energy means — and why the charger gets warm even though that heat isn’t doing any useful work?

1044.desc: Identify the main energy stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electromagnetic) and the pathways by which energy is transferred between stores (mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation)
1044.ev: Names and describes at least five energy stores with a real-world example of each
1044.q: If {{name}} watched a ball being thrown upward and then falling back down, could they describe what type of energy the ball has at the top of its arc and at the bottom — and explain what happened to the energy between those two points?

1048.desc: Explain that sound is produced by vibrating objects and travels as a longitudinal pressure wave through solids, liquids, and gases; describe reflection of sound (echoes) and absorption; explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum
1048.ev: Explains how a vibrating object creates regions of compression and rarefaction in air
1048.q: If {{name}} heard an echo in a large empty hall, could they explain what causes the echo, why the same sound in a carpeted living room doesn’t echo, and what would happen to sound in outer space?

1050.desc: Describe magnetic poles (north and south), explain attraction and repulsion between poles, describe magnetic field lines plotted using a compass, and explain the Earth's magnetic field and its practical uses
1050.ev: States the rule for attraction and repulsion of magnetic poles
1050.q: If {{name}} used a compass and iron filings to map the magnetic field around a bar magnet, could they describe what pattern the field lines make and explain why a compass needle always points roughly north?

1052.desc: Distinguish between mass (amount of matter, measured in kg) and weight (gravitational force, measured in N), use the equation weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and explain why g differs on other planets and stars
1052.ev: Explains the difference between mass and weight with correct units for each
1052.q: If {{name}} weighed themselves on bathroom scales and was then asked what they would weigh on the Moon, could they explain the difference between mass and weight and work out a rough answer?

1057.desc: State the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and explain refraction as the change in speed and direction when light crosses a boundary between two media; apply ray diagrams for plane mirrors and refracting surfaces
1057.ev: States the law of reflection and applies it to draw a reflected ray correctly
1057.q: If {{name}} put a straw in a glass of water and it looked bent at the surface, could they explain why that happens — drawing a diagram to show the path of light at the water’s surface?

1058.desc: Explain relative motion — how the apparent speed and direction of an object depends on the observer's own motion — using everyday examples such as trains and cars passing
1058.ev: Explains why a train moving at the same speed in the same direction as another appears stationary to passengers on that train
1058.q: If {{name}} was on a train and another train passed going the same direction but faster, could they explain why it looks slow even if it's actually travelling at high speed?

1062.desc: Describe forces as vector quantities with both magnitude and direction, distinguish between balanced forces (zero resultant, no change in motion) and unbalanced forces (non-zero resultant, causes acceleration or deceleration)
1062.ev: Explains what a vector quantity is and why force is a vector
1062.q: If {{name}} was pushing a heavy box along the floor but it wasn't moving, could they explain all the forces acting on it and why it stays still even though you're pushing?

124.desc: Calculate average speed using the equation speed = distance ÷ time, represent journeys on distance-time graphs, and interpret gradient as speed and flat sections as stationary periods
124.ev: Uses speed = distance ÷ time to calculate average speed with correct units (m/s, km/h)
124.q: If {{name}} tracked a cycle ride on a map and knew how far they went and how long it took, could they calculate the average speed — and then sketch a rough graph showing the journey including a stop for lunch?

795.desc: Explain static electricity as the build-up of electric charge through friction, describe how charged objects attract or repel each other, and relate static discharge to everyday phenomena such as lightning
795.ev: Explains that rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another, creating opposite charges
795.q: Can {{name}} explain why a balloon rubbed on hair sticks to the wall, and connect this to the science of how lightning forms during a thunderstorm?

1046.desc: Describe waves in terms of amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave speed; distinguish transverse waves (oscillation perpendicular to direction of travel) from longitudinal waves (oscillation parallel); and use the wave equation v = fλ
1046.ev: Labels a wave diagram with amplitude, wavelength, crest, and trough
1046.q: If {{name}} was asked to describe a wave and how fast it travels, could they sketch one, label the wavelength and amplitude, and use the wave equation to work out speed from the frequency and wavelength?

1020.desc: Explain that white light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV), describe dispersion through a prism, explain why objects appear coloured (selective reflection and absorption of wavelengths), and describe colour mixing with filters
1020.ev: Lists the colours of the visible spectrum in order of increasing frequency
1020.q: If {{name}} shone white light through a prism, could they explain why a rainbow of colours appears — and then predict what colour a blue jumper would look under red light and why?

1067.desc: Describe how the energy carried by a wave increases with its amplitude, linking louder sounds and brighter light to larger amplitudes
1067.ev: States that larger amplitude means more energy carried
1067.q: If {{name}} is shown two waves with the same wavelength but different heights, can they say which carries more energy and why?

1068.desc: Explain charging by friction as the transfer of electrons from one material to another, so one object becomes negative and the other equally positive, with total charge conserved
1068.ev: Explains which object gains electrons when a balloon is rubbed on hair
1068.q: If {{name}} rubs a balloon on a jumper and it becomes negative, can they explain what happened to the jumper and why?

1069.desc: Describe and compare the three mechanisms of heat transfer — conduction (particle vibration through solids), convection (fluid movement in liquids/gases), and radiation (infrared waves) — and explain that the rate of transfer depends on temperature difference
1069.ev: Explains the particle-level mechanism for conduction and why metals are good conductors
1069.q: If {{name}} was heating soup on a hob and also warming their hands by a radiator, could they explain which type of heat transfer is happening in each case — and why the soup pot gets hot throughout even though it’s only heated at the bottom?

1070.desc: Explain forces associated with deforming objects (elastic and inelastic deformation), thermal expansion and contraction of materials, and how fluid pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth
1070.ev: Distinguishes elastic deformation (returns to shape) from inelastic/plastic deformation (permanently changed)
1070.q: If {{name}} noticed the lid on a jar was very tight, could they explain why running it under hot water helps — and what's happening to the metal as it heats up?

1071.desc: Design, test and improve a device that minimises or maximises thermal energy transfer (e.g. an insulated cup or a solar cooker), controlling variables and measuring temperature change
1071.ev: Chooses materials based on conduction, convection and radiation
1071.q: If {{name}} is challenged to keep an ice cube from melting for as long as possible, can they design a container and explain how each part reduces heat transfer?

1053.desc: Draw ray diagrams to show reflection at a plane mirror (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and refraction at a boundary between media; use ray diagrams to locate images and explain how lenses and mirrors work
1053.ev: Draw a ray diagram for a plane mirror showing the incident ray, normal, reflected ray, and virtual image
1053.q: Can {{name}} draw a diagram showing how a ray of light bounces off a mirror or bends when it passes from air into glass — labelling the angles correctly?

1072.desc: Calculate energy efficiency as the ratio of useful output energy to total input energy, construct and interpret Sankey diagrams, and calculate work done using work = force × distance
1072.ev: Calculates efficiency as a percentage from given input and useful output energy values
1072.q: If {{name}} heard that a light bulb is 10% efficient and uses 60 J of energy, could they work out how much of that energy actually becomes light — and where the rest goes?

1073.desc: Describe the magnetic effect of an electric current (a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field), and investigate how the strength of an electromagnet depends on current, number of coil turns, and core material
1073.ev: Describes that a current-carrying wire produces a circular magnetic field
1073.q: If {{name}} built an electromagnet using a battery, wire, and iron nail, could they describe two ways to make it pick up more paperclips — and explain why it stops working when the circuit is switched off?

1074.desc: Identify the four ways energy is transferred between stores — mechanically (by a force doing work), electrically (by a current), by heating, and by radiation (light and other electromagnetic waves) — noting that sound also carries energy as a mechanical wave, and describe a chain of transfers for a familiar device
1074.q: If {{name}} switches on a battery torch, can they describe the energy stores and how energy moves between them until it lights the room?

1075.desc: Explain that lifting an object stores energy in the gravitational store, and that the amount depends on its mass, its height and the strength of gravity
1075.ev: Predicts which of two objects stores more gravitational potential energy
1075.q: If {{name}} carries a heavy bag up the stairs, can they explain where the energy they used has gone and how it could be got back?

1076.desc: Plan and carry out experiments to measure energy transferred during heating, including using the equation Q = mcΔT, recording temperature changes over time, and evaluating sources of error
1076.ev: Uses a thermometer and stopwatch to record temperature change over time in a heating experiment
1076.q: If {{name}} heated 100 ml of water in a beaker and recorded the temperature every minute, could they plot the results on a graph and use the data to work out roughly how much energy was transferred to the water?

1079.desc: Plan and carry out investigations into forces, including measuring force with a newton meter, investigating Hooke's Law, and collecting and interpreting motion data to test Newton's laws
1079.ev: Uses a newton meter correctly to measure forces in newtons
1079.q: If {{name}} set up an experiment hanging weights on a spring and measuring how much it stretched, could they describe how they would make it a fair test, record the results, and show what Hooke's Law looks like on a graph?

1080.desc: Explain, using data, that an object's kinetic energy increases with its mass and increases much more steeply with its speed (doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy)
1080.ev: Predicts which of two objects has more kinetic energy from mass and speed
1080.q: If {{name}} compares a car at 30 mph with the same car at 60 mph, can they explain why the faster car carries far more than twice the energy?

1078.desc: Calculate the turning effect (moment = force × perpendicular distance), explain how pressure is transmitted equally in liquids (Pascal's principle) and the concept of atmospheric pressure, and describe Hooke's Law (extension ∝ force up to the elastic limit)
1078.ev: Calculates the moment of a force and uses the principle of moments to solve lever problems
1078.q: If {{name}} was using a long spanner to loosen a tight bolt, could they explain why a longer spanner makes it easier — and work out what force would be needed with a spanner of a specific length?

1077.desc: State and apply Newton's First Law (an object stays at rest or constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force) and Second Law (force = mass × acceleration), including the relationship between mass, force, and acceleration
1077.ev: States Newton's First Law and gives a real example (e.g. why a moving spacecraft doesn't need engines in space)
1077.q: If {{name}} was asked why you need a seatbelt in a car but not when sitting still, could they explain what Newton's First Law says about moving objects — and then calculate how much force a 60 kg person experiences in a sudden stop?

1083.desc: State and apply Newton's Third Law: every force has an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object, distinguishing action-reaction pairs from balanced forces
1083.ev: States Newton's Third Law correctly, identifying both the action and reaction force and the objects they act on
1083.q: If {{name}} saw a video of a rocket launching into space, could they explain what force is pushing the rocket upward and where that force comes from — and which law of motion that demonstrates?

1084.desc: Apply Ohm's Law (V = IR) to calculate current, voltage, or resistance in a simple circuit, and explain that resistance opposes the flow of current
1084.ev: States Ohm's Law as V = IR and identifies the units for each quantity
1084.q: If {{name}} doubles the resistance in a circuit while keeping the battery the same, can they predict what happens to the current and explain using the V = IR formula?

1085.desc: Define power as the rate of energy transfer (power = energy ÷ time, measured in watts), and compare energy transfer rates in different everyday contexts
1085.ev: States the definition of power and gives its unit (watt)
1085.q: If {{name}} was comparing a 100 W light bulb with a 10 W LED, could they explain what those numbers mean and calculate how much energy each uses in an hour?

1086.desc: Construct ray diagrams to show the formation of images by plane mirrors and converging lenses, identifying whether images are real or virtual, magnified or diminished, upright or inverted
1086.ev: Draws an accurate ray diagram for a plane mirror showing a virtual, upright, same-size image
1086.q: If {{name}} was asked to show on a diagram where their reflection appears to be when they look in a mirror, could they draw the correct ray paths and explain whether the image is real or virtual — and where it actually appears to be located?

1087.desc: Read amplitude and wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and amplitude and period from a displacement–time graph, and explain what each axis shows
1087.ev: Measures amplitude and wavelength from a displacement–distance graph
1087.q: If {{name}} is given a displacement–time graph of a wave, can they read off its amplitude and its period, with units?

930.desc: Distinguish between renewable energy resources (solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomass) and non-renewable resources (coal, oil, gas, nuclear), comparing their advantages, disadvantages, and environmental impacts
930.ev: Lists at least four renewable and three non-renewable energy resources
930.q: If {{name}} heard about a plan to build a new wind farm in your area, could they explain what the advantages and disadvantages would be compared to a gas-fired power station — both for the environment and for reliability?

1088.desc: Describe and apply the rules for current, voltage, and resistance in series and parallel circuits, and explain the practical uses of each circuit type
1088.ev: States the rules for current and voltage in series circuits (current same everywhere; voltages add up)
1088.q: Can {{name}} explain why the lights in your home don't all switch off when you turn off one room's light, but a string of old-fashioned Christmas lights does go off if one bulb breaks?

1089.desc: Distinguish temperature (average particle kinetic energy) from the total thermal energy of an object, which also depends on how much matter it contains and what it is made of
1089.ev: Explains why a bath of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water
1089.q: If {{name}} compares a cup of boiling water with a bath of warm water, can they explain which has more thermal energy and why that's different from which is hotter?

860.desc: Describe the full electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays, in order of increasing frequency and energy; explain that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; and describe the uses and hazards of different regions
860.ev: Lists the seven regions of the EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency
860.q: If {{name}} heard about microwaves, X-rays, and visible light all being part of the same family, could they explain what makes them different from each other and name one useful application and one risk for each?

1091.desc: Connect ammeters in series and voltmeters in parallel, read analogue and digital meters with suitable ranges, and check for zero errors
1091.ev: Draws a circuit with an ammeter and a voltmeter correctly placed
1091.q: If {{name}} wants to measure the current through and voltage across a lamp, can they draw where each meter goes and explain why?

1092.desc: Explain how waves can be absorbed, transmitted, or reflected by different materials, and apply these interactions to explain colour perception, sight, communication technologies, and the effects of different surfaces on wave behaviour
1092.ev: Explains the difference between absorption, transmission, and reflection of waves
1092.q: If {{name}} was wearing a black t-shirt on a sunny day and a friend was wearing white, could they explain using wave interactions why the black shirt gets hotter — and which properties of materials determine how they absorb or reflect radiation?

1065.desc: Explain that a wave transfers energy (and information) from one place to another while the particles of the medium only oscillate about fixed positions, using evidence such as a floating cork bobbing on ripples
1065.ev: Explains why a cork on a pond moves up and down but not along with the ripples
1065.q: If {{name}} watches a duck bobbing as ripples pass, can they explain why the duck isn't carried across the pond?

1094.desc: Distinguish analog signals, which vary continuously, from digital signals, which take only a few discrete values (often 0 and 1), using examples such as vinyl records and streamed music
1094.ev: Sketches an analog and a digital signal
1094.q: If {{name}} compares a vinyl record and a music file, can they explain how the sound is stored differently?

1097.desc: Calculate the net (resultant) force on an object in one dimension by adding forces with signs for direction, and predict whether the object speeds up, slows down or keeps a constant velocity
1097.ev: Calculates the resultant of opposing forces
1097.q: If {{name}} sees a 500 N driving force and 350 N of drag on a car, can they work out the net force and say what happens to the car's speed?

936.desc: Use the wave equation v = f × λ to calculate wave speed, frequency or wavelength, rearranging as needed and using correct units
936.ev: Calculates the speed of a wave from its frequency and wavelength
936.q: If {{name}} is told a sound wave has a frequency of 680 Hz and travels at 340 m/s, can they find its wavelength?

1098.desc: Describe a longitudinal wave in terms of compressions and rarefactions of the medium, identify the wavelength on a longitudinal diagram, and model it with a slinky
1098.ev: Labels compressions and rarefactions on a diagram
1098.q: If {{name}} pushes and pulls one end of a slinky, can they point to a compression and a rarefaction and show one wavelength?

1099.desc: Explain conduction in solids as vibrating particles passing energy to neighbours, and why metals conduct so well (free electrons), while gases are poor conductors
1099.ev: Describes conduction as particle-to-particle energy transfer
1099.q: If {{name}} holds a metal spoon in hot soup, can they explain how the heat travels up the spoon to their hand?

1100.desc: Explain convection currents as warmer fluid expanding, becoming less dense and rising while cooler, denser fluid sinks, and apply this to heaters, sea breezes and the atmosphere
1100.ev: Explains why warm air rises using density
1100.q: If {{name}} sees a radiator under a window, can they draw how air moves around the room and explain why using density?

1101.desc: Explain that conventional current is shown flowing from positive to negative while electrons actually drift from negative to positive, and why the convention persists
1101.ev: Marks conventional current on a circuit diagram
1101.q: If {{name}} sees an arrow showing current leaving the positive terminal, can they explain which way the electrons are moving?

760.desc: Interpret cooling curves — steep at first and levelling off as the object approaches room temperature — and explain how temperature difference, insulation thickness, material and surface area change the rate of heat loss
760.ev: Explains why a hot drink cools fastest at first
760.q: If {{name}} records the temperature of a cup of tea every minute, can they explain why it cools quickly at first and more slowly later?

1102.desc: Choose the system being studied, draw its boundary, and track energy flowing into and out of it — recognising that a closed system's total energy stays constant, while an open system can gain or lose energy
1102.ev: Draws a boundary around a chosen system (e.g. kettle + water)
1102.q: If {{name}} is describing a pan of water heating on a stove, can they say what they're counting as 'the system' and which energy transfers go in or out of it?

1095.desc: Draw free-body diagrams for a single object showing every force acting on it as a labelled arrow from the object, with lengths showing relative size, and use them to find the resultant force
1095.ev: Draws all forces on a single object (weight, normal, friction, tension, drag)
1095.q: If {{name}} draws a book resting on a table, can they show every force on the book and explain why it doesn't move?

1103.desc: Define frequency as the number of waves passing a point per second (hertz) and time period as the time for one wave, and convert between them using f = 1/T
1103.ev: Calculates the frequency of a wave with a period of 0.02 s
1103.q: If {{name}} knows a wave has a period of 0.25 s, can they work out its frequency and explain what that number means?

1105.desc: State that humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, define ultrasound and infrasound by frequency, and compare hearing ranges of animals and of people as they age
1105.ev: States the approximate human hearing range in Hz
1105.q: If {{name}} is told a bat calls at 50 000 Hz, can they explain why people cannot hear it?

1106.desc: Explain inertia as an object's tendency to resist changes in its motion, with mass as its measure, and use it to explain seatbelts, headrests and why heavy objects are hard to start and stop
1106.q: If {{name}} pulls a tablecloth quickly from under some plates, can they explain why the plates stay put?

900.desc: Explain that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, that hotter objects emit more, and that dark matt surfaces are better emitters and absorbers than light shiny ones
900.ev: Ranks surfaces by how well they absorb and emit infrared
900.q: If {{name}} is asked why marathon runners are wrapped in shiny foil blankets, can they explain how it keeps them warm?

1107.desc: Explain the motor effect as the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and describe how this principle is used in electric motors and loudspeakers
1107.ev: Explains that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (the motor effect)
1107.q: If {{name}} looked inside an electric motor or the back of a loudspeaker, could they explain why the coil of wire moves — and what would happen to the movement if you reversed the direction of the current?

1109.desc: Distinguish permanent magnets from induced magnets that become magnetic only in a field, and explain that induced magnetism always attracts and is lost when the field is removed
1109.ev: Explains why a paper clip sticks to a magnet and to another clip
1109.q: If {{name}} hangs a chain of paper clips from a magnet, can they explain what happens when the magnet is removed?

399.desc: Distinguish scalar quantities (magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, energy) from vector quantities (magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, force, acceleration), and represent vectors as arrows
399.ev: Classifies quantities as scalar or vector
399.q: If {{name}} runs one full lap of a 400 m track, can they explain why their distance is 400 m but their displacement is zero?

869.desc: Explain specific heat capacity as the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, compare materials, and use it to explain why water heats and cools slowly and moderates coastal climates
869.ev: Defines specific heat capacity with units J/kg°C
869.q: If {{name}} notices sand on a beach is scorching while the sea is still cool, can they explain why using specific heat capacity?

495.desc: Distinguish specular reflection from smooth surfaces (which forms images) from diffuse reflection from rough surfaces (which scatters light), applying the law of reflection at each point
495.ev: Draws rays reflecting from a smooth and a rough surface
495.q: If {{name}} compares a mirror and a sheet of white paper, can they explain why only one shows their reflection even though both reflect light?

1110.desc: Recognise and draw symbols for resistors, variable resistors, diodes, LEDs, LDRs, thermistors, fuses, ammeters and voltmeters, and build circuits from diagrams
1110.ev: Draws the symbols for an LDR and a thermistor
1110.q: If {{name}} is given a circuit diagram with a thermistor and an LED, can they name every component and build it?

1111.desc: Explain that energy dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings spreads out thinly over many particles, so although none is destroyed it becomes much harder to use again — the idea behind 'wasted' energy
1111.ev: Identifies where energy is dissipated in a device
1111.q: If {{name}} notices a phone charger getting warm, can they explain what's happening to some of the energy and why it isn't destroyed?

715.desc: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity (a = Δv/t, in m/s²), including deceleration as negative acceleration, and calculate it from data
715.ev: Calculates acceleration from change in velocity and time
715.q: If {{name}} is told a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds, can they work out its acceleration and explain what the number means?
