1113.desc: Distinguish direct current from cells and batteries from alternating current from the mains, and state mains frequency and voltage (230 V at 50 Hz in the UK; 120 V at 60 Hz in the US)
1113.ev: Sketches pd–time graphs for ac and dc
1113.q: If {{name}} looks at an oscilloscope trace from a battery and from a mains adapter's input, can they say which is ac and why?

1114.desc: Use F = ma with the net force to solve multi-step problems — finding acceleration from several forces, or the force needed for a given acceleration — and link to the equations of motion
1114.ev: Calculates acceleration from net force and mass
1114.q: If {{name}} is told a 1200 kg car has a 3000 N engine force and 600 N of resistance, can they work out its acceleration?

1115.desc: Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy using ΔGPE = mgh, with g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth, and rearrange to find height or mass
1115.ev: Calculates GPE change for a lifted object
1115.q: If {{name}} lifts a 2 kg box onto a shelf 1.5 m high, can they calculate how much gravitational potential energy it gained?

917.desc: Calculate kinetic energy using KE = ½mv², with mass in kg and speed in m/s, and rearrange to find mass or speed
917.ev: Calculates KE for given mass and speed with units of joules
917.q: If {{name}} knows a 60 kg cyclist is travelling at 5 m/s, can they work out the cyclist's kinetic energy?

1116.desc: Explain that pressure in a liquid increases with depth and density (p = ρgh), and use it to explain dams, diving and upthrust
1116.ev: Calculates pressure at a given depth
1116.q: If {{name}} dives to the bottom of a swimming pool and feels their ears hurt, can they explain why pressure is greater there?

1117.desc: Describe how converging (convex) and diverging (concave) lenses refract parallel rays, define principal focus and focal length, and use lens symbols in diagrams
1117.ev: Draws parallel rays passing through each type of lens
1117.q: If {{name}} holds a magnifying glass in sunlight, can they explain where the bright spot forms and what that distance is called?

1118.desc: Define current as the rate of flow of charge and use Q = I × t to calculate charge in coulombs, current in amperes or time
1118.ev: Calculates charge passing in a given time
1118.q: If {{name}} knows 2 A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes, can they calculate how much charge has passed?

1119.desc: Explain that a diode lets current flow in one direction only, that an LED is a diode that emits light, and why LEDs are more efficient than filament bulbs
1119.ev: Predicts whether a lamp lights with a diode either way round
1119.q: If {{name}} puts a diode in a circuit the wrong way round, can they predict what happens and explain why?

1112.desc: Use displacement and velocity as signed quantities in one dimension, choosing a positive direction, and calculate average velocity as displacement ÷ time
1112.ev: Chooses a positive direction and uses negative values for the opposite way
1112.q: If {{name}} walks 30 m east then 10 m west in 20 s, can they work out their average speed and their average velocity?

1120.desc: Use echoes to measure distances with distance = speed × time ÷ 2, as in sonar and echo-sounding, explaining why the time is halved
1120.ev: Calculates the depth of the sea from a sonar echo time
1120.q: If {{name}} hears an echo from a cliff 2 s after shouting, can they work out how far away the cliff is if sound travels at 340 m/s?

1017.desc: Describe the electric field around a charged object, draw field lines for isolated charges, and explain that a charge in the field feels a force that is stronger closer to the object, causing sparks when the field is strong enough
1017.ev: Draws field lines around a positive and a negative charge
1017.q: If {{name}} brings a small charged ball near a charged dome, can they describe the field and predict the force on the ball?

1121.desc: Explain how electromagnets are used in relays, electric bells, door locks and scrapyard cranes, and why they are useful because they can be switched off
1121.ev: Explains how a relay lets a small current switch a large one
1121.q: If {{name}} looks at a relay in a car starter circuit, can they explain how the small switch controls the big motor current?

1122.desc: Calculate energy transferred by appliances using E = P × t in both joules and kilowatt-hours, and use unit prices to work out running costs
1122.ev: Calculates energy in kWh from power in kW and time in hours
1122.q: If {{name}} runs a 2 kW heater for 3 hours and electricity costs 30p per kWh, can they work out how much it costs?

1124.desc: Explain refraction as a change in speed at a boundary that makes wavefronts change direction, bending towards the normal when the wave slows down, with no change of direction along the normal
1124.ev: Draws wavefronts bending as they enter a slower medium
1124.q: If {{name}} shines a ray into a glass block at an angle, can they explain with wavefronts why it bends towards the normal?

1125.desc: Use systematic reasoning and meter readings to locate faults such as open circuits, short circuits and blown components
1125.ev: Predicts meter readings for an open circuit
1125.q: If {{name}} has a series circuit where nothing lights, can they explain how to use a voltmeter to find the broken part?

768.desc: Investigate Hooke's law (F = ke), plot force–extension graphs, find the spring constant from the gradient and identify the limit of proportionality
768.q: If {{name}} hangs weights on a spring and records its extension, can they find the spring constant from a graph?

1126.desc: Explain that without air resistance all objects near Earth's surface fall with the same acceleration (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²), regardless of mass, and calculate speeds of falling objects
1126.ev: States that a hammer and feather fall together in a vacuum
1126.q: If {{name}} drops a bowling ball and a tennis ball from the same height, can they predict which lands first and explain why?

1127.desc: Describe how the resistance of a light-dependent resistor falls as light increases and how a thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises, with uses in automatic lights and thermostats
1127.ev: States how each component's resistance changes
1127.q: If {{name}} is designing a night light, can they explain which component senses the dark and how its resistance changes?

1128.desc: Identify the live, neutral and earth wires and their functions, and explain how the earth wire and fuse protect people when a fault makes a metal case live
1128.ev: States the function of each wire in a three-core cable
1128.q: If {{name}} is told a kettle's metal case has become live, can they explain how the earth wire and fuse keep them safe?

1130.desc: Plan and carry out methods to measure wave speed — timing an echo or using two microphones for sound, and measuring frequency and wavelength in a ripple tank — and evaluate sources of error
1130.ev: Describes a method to measure the speed of sound in air
1130.q: If {{name}} has two microphones and a timer, can they describe how to measure the speed of sound and what would make the result unreliable?

1131.desc: Define momentum as mass × velocity (p = mv, in kg m/s), recognise it as a vector, and compare the momentum of different objects
1131.q: If {{name}} compares a 2000 kg truck at 5 m/s with a 70 kg cyclist at 10 m/s, can they work out which has more momentum?

1132.desc: Define potential difference as the energy transferred per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C) and use V = E/Q
1132.ev: Explains what 12 V means in joules and coulombs
1132.q: If {{name}} is told a battery is 9 V, can they explain what that means for each coulomb of charge?

1133.desc: Explain how lubrication, insulation, streamlining and better design reduce unwanted energy transfers and increase efficiency, and evaluate trade-offs such as cost
1133.ev: Explains how lubrication reduces dissipation by friction
1133.q: If {{name}} is asked how to make a bicycle more efficient, can they suggest two changes and explain what wasted energy each one reduces?

1134.desc: Calculate total resistance in series (R = R₁ + R₂ + …), explain that current is the same everywhere and that the supply pd is shared in proportion to resistance
1134.ev: Calculates total resistance of resistors in series
1134.q: If {{name}} has a 6 V battery with 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in series, can they find the current and the pd across each?

1135.desc: State that all electromagnetic waves are transverse, travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, need no medium and transfer energy, differing only in wavelength and frequency
1135.ev: Lists the properties all EM waves share
1135.q: If {{name}} is asked how radio waves and X-rays are alike, can they list what all electromagnetic waves have in common?

1136.desc: Interpret oscilloscope or microphone traces of sounds — taller traces are louder, more closely packed traces are higher pitched — and calculate frequency from the time base
1136.ev: Compares two traces for loudness and pitch
1136.q: If {{name}} sees two oscilloscope traces of notes, can they say which is louder, which is higher, and estimate one frequency from the time base?

1137.desc: Explain stopping distance as thinking distance plus braking distance, and how speed, reaction time, road conditions and vehicle condition affect each
1137.q: If {{name}} is told a driver is tired and the road is wet, can they explain which part of the stopping distance each one affects?

1138.desc: Explain that when objects at different temperatures are in contact in a closed system, energy transfers from hotter to colder until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium)
1138.ev: Predicts the direction of energy transfer between two objects
1138.q: If {{name}} drops a hot metal spoon into a cold drink, can they describe what happens to the temperatures of both until they stop changing?

1139.desc: Explain dangers of static (sparks when refuelling, shocks) and how earthing prevents them, and describe uses such as electrostatic spray painting, photocopiers and smoke precipitators
1139.ev: Explains why fuel tankers are earthed
1139.q: If {{name}} sees a fuel tanker connected by a wire to the ground before refuelling, can they explain why?

941.desc: Explain why each region of the spectrum suits its uses — radio for broadcasting, microwaves for satellites and cooking, infrared for heating and remote controls, visible light in fibres, UV for sterilising, X-rays and gamma for imaging and treatment
941.ev: Matches each region to a use
941.q: If {{name}} is asked why X-rays are used for broken bones, can they explain using what X-rays do to bone and to soft tissue?

710.desc: Draw and interpret velocity–time graphs, using the gradient to find acceleration and the area under the graph to find displacement
710.ev: Identifies constant velocity, acceleration and deceleration sections
710.q: If {{name}} sees a velocity–time graph of a train leaving a station, can they find its acceleration and how far it travelled in the first 20 seconds?

1123.desc: Explain that a wave's speed depends on the medium it travels through — sound is fastest in solids and cannot cross a vacuum, light is slower in glass than in air — and that at a boundary the frequency stays the same while the wavelength changes
1123.ev: Orders the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases
1123.q: If {{name}} hears that sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, can they say what happens to its wavelength when it passes from air into water?

1140.desc: Investigate how a wire's length, thickness, material and temperature affect its resistance, controlling variables and plotting resistance against length
1140.ev: Predicts how doubling length changes resistance
1140.q: If {{name}} measures the resistance of 20 cm, 40 cm and 60 cm of the same wire, can they predict the pattern and explain it?

1141.desc: Explain that noise added during transmission can be removed from digital signals by regenerating clean pulses, whereas noise in analog signals is amplified with the signal
1141.ev: Shows on a sketch how noise affects each type of signal
1141.q: If {{name}} hears crackle on an old analog radio but not on digital radio, can they explain the difference?

1142.desc: Explain why appliances in homes are connected in parallel — each gets the full mains pd and can be switched independently — and what happens to total current as more appliances are switched on
1142.ev: Explains two advantages of parallel wiring at home
1142.q: If {{name}} plugs a heater, kettle and toaster into one extension lead, can they explain why the total current could become dangerous?

459.desc: Add perpendicular vectors using Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry, and resolve a force or velocity into horizontal and vertical components
459.ev: Finds the resultant of two perpendicular forces
459.q: If {{name}} swims across a river at 2 m/s while the current flows at 1 m/s, can they find their actual speed and direction?

1145.desc: Compare an alternator (slip rings, ac output) with a dynamo (split-ring commutator, dc output) and sketch their output graphs, explaining how speed affects frequency and peak voltage
1145.q: If {{name}} turns a bicycle dynamo faster, can they sketch how its output changes?

1146.desc: Use v = fλ with the speed of light to calculate frequencies and wavelengths across the spectrum, working in standard form
1146.ev: Calculates the wavelength of a 100 MHz radio wave
1146.q: If {{name}} is told a radio station broadcasts at 98 MHz, can they calculate the wavelength?

1148.desc: Explain how communication systems choose wave types to carry information — radio and microwaves for wireless and satellite links, light in optical fibres — and how signals are encoded on a carrier wave
1148.q: If {{name}} is asked why internet cables under the sea use optical fibre, can they explain the advantages?

1150.desc: Calculate the normal current of an appliance from I = P/V and choose a suitable fuse rating, and compare fuses, circuit breakers and residual current devices
1150.ev: Calculates the current for a 2 kW kettle on 230 V
1150.q: If {{name}} has a 1200 W hair dryer on 230 V mains, can they choose the right fuse and explain why?

863.desc: Use data on cost per kWh, reliability, land use and carbon emissions to compare energy resources and argue for an energy mix
863.ev: Calculates and compares cost or emissions per kWh
863.q: If {{name}} is given data on wind, gas and nuclear power, can they compare them on cost and carbon and argue for a sensible mix?

1153.desc: Use conservation of momentum (total momentum before = after when no external force acts) to calculate velocities after collisions in one dimension
1153.ev: States the conservation of momentum principle
1153.q: If {{name}} sees a moving trolley hit and stick to a stationary one of equal mass, can they predict the speed afterwards?

1156.desc: Design, build and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another within constraints (e.g. a solar oven, wind turbine or generator), measuring input and output to evaluate efficiency
1156.ev: Defines criteria and constraints for the device
1156.q: If {{name}} builds a small wind turbine for a school project, can they explain how they would measure how well it works and decide what to improve?

1158.desc: Design, evaluate and refine a device that minimises the force on an object during a collision (e.g. egg-drop protector, helmet, crumple zone), using impulse reasoning and test data
1158.ev: Uses impulse ideas to justify design choices
1158.q: If {{name}} designs a package to protect an egg dropped from a height, can they explain the physics of why their design works?

1159.desc: Describe diffraction as the spreading of waves through gaps and around obstacles, greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength, and use it to explain why sound bends round doorways but light does not noticeably
1159.ev: Sketches wavefronts passing through narrow and wide gaps
1159.q: If {{name}} can hear someone talking in the next room but can't see them, can they use wavelengths to explain why?

769.desc: Calculate the energy stored in a stretched spring using E = ½ke² (within the limit of proportionality) and relate it to the area under a force–extension graph
769.ev: Calculates elastic energy from spring constant and extension
769.q: If {{name}} stretches a spring with spring constant 200 N/m by 0.1 m, can they work out how much energy it stores?

1149.desc: Calculate electrical power and energy transferred using P = IV, P = I²R and E = QV, and explain why power is transmitted at high voltage
1149.ev: Calculates power from current and potential difference
1149.q: If {{name}} knows a kettle draws 10 A from a 230 V supply, can they work out its power?

1161.desc: Model the energy of a macroscopic object as the sum of energy from the motion of its particles (kinetic) and their relative positions (potential), explaining thermal energy and changes of state in these terms
1161.ev: Explains thermal energy as particle kinetic plus potential energy
1161.q: If {{name}} rubs their hands together and they get warm, can they explain what has happened to the energy in terms of particles?

1162.desc: Use conservation of energy to solve problems where energy transfers between kinetic and gravitational stores (falling objects, pendulums, roller coasters), such as finding speed from height using mgh = ½mv²
1162.ev: Equates GPE lost to KE gained for a falling object
1162.q: If {{name}} drops a ball from 5 m, can they use energy ideas to work out how fast it is going just before it hits the ground?

1160.desc: Explain that energy can be stored when objects interact through a field at a distance — gravitational, magnetic or electric — and that this energy changes as the objects move closer or further apart
1160.ev: Describes energy changes as two magnets are pushed together or pulled apart
1160.q: If {{name}} pushes the like poles of two magnets together and lets go, can they explain where the energy that makes them spring apart was stored?

1155.desc: Trace the energy chain in a thermal power station (fuel → thermal → kinetic in turbine → electrical) and in renewable alternatives, identifying where energy is dissipated
1155.ev: Describes each stage of a thermal power station
1155.q: If {{name}} is asked how burning gas ends up lighting a lamp in their house, can they describe each energy transfer along the way?

1164.desc: Use the equations of motion for constant acceleration (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t), choosing the right one and rearranging to find unknowns
1164.ev: Lists known and unknown quantities before choosing an equation
1164.q: If {{name}} is told a car accelerates from 10 m/s at 2 m/s² for 5 s, can they find its final speed and how far it travelled?

1163.desc: Explain non-contact forces using fields — gravitational, electric and magnetic — drawing field-line diagrams and describing field strength and direction
1163.ev: Draws field lines around a magnet, a charge and a planet
1163.q: If {{name}} sees iron filings around a bar magnet, can they explain what the pattern tells them about the magnetic field?

1165.desc: Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a wire carrying current in a magnetic field, and calculate it with F = BIL
1165.ev: Uses the left-hand rule to predict force direction
1165.q: If {{name}} sees a wire jump upwards between magnet poles, can they use the left-hand rule to check the current direction?

1167.desc: Model friction as depending on the normal force and the surfaces, distinguish static friction (up to a maximum) from kinetic friction, and use F ≤ μN in simple problems
1167.ev: Explains what the normal force is
1167.q: If {{name}} pushes a heavy box that won't move at first, then suddenly slides, can they explain what is happening to the friction force?

1143.desc: Explain that moving a magnet near a coil (or a coil in a magnetic field) induces a current, and that generators in power stations use this to transform kinetic energy into electrical energy
1143.ev: Describes how to induce a current with a magnet and coil
1143.q: If {{name}} moves a magnet in and out of a coil connected to a meter, can they explain why the needle flicks and how that relates to a power station?

1144.desc: Explain how forces on opposite sides of a coil make it turn, why a split-ring commutator is needed to keep it turning, and how to make the motor faster
1144.ev: Explains why the forces on opposite sides form a turning effect
1144.q: If {{name}} builds a simple motor that rocks back and forth instead of spinning, can they explain what part is missing?

1169.desc: Describe the National Grid as a network linking power stations to consumers, with step-up transformers to very high voltages for transmission and step-down transformers for safe use
1169.ev: Draws a labelled block diagram of the grid
1169.q: If {{name}} follows electricity from a power station to a socket, can they describe each stage and why the voltage changes?

1168.desc: Explain how an alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in an iron core that induces an alternating pd in the secondary, and why transformers do not work with dc
1168.ev: Labels primary coil, secondary coil and core
1168.q: If {{name}} connects a transformer to a battery, can they explain why the bulb on the secondary only flickers at switch-on?

1157.desc: Relate force to change in momentum (FΔt = Δp, so F = Δp/Δt), and explain why increasing collision time reduces force
1157.ev: Uses F = Δp/Δt to calculate an average force
1157.q: If {{name}} is asked why it hurts less to land on a crash mat than on concrete, can they explain using momentum and time?

706.desc: Find the speed at a particular instant from a curved distance–time graph by drawing a tangent and calculating its gradient, distinguishing it from average speed
706.ev: Draws a tangent to a curve at a point
706.q: If {{name}} has a curved distance–time graph for a sprinter, can they find how fast the sprinter was going exactly 3 seconds in?

992.desc: Explain that higher-frequency EM radiation carries more energy, that UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage cells, and that lower-frequency radiation mainly causes heating
992.q: If {{name}} is asked why sunscreen blocks UV but nobody worries about radio waves, can they explain the difference?

1171.desc: Obtain and interpret current–voltage graphs for a fixed resistor (straight line through origin), a filament lamp (curve) and a diode (current one way only), explaining each shape
1171.ev: Sketches the I–V graph for each component
1171.q: If {{name}} is shown three I–V graphs, can they match each to a resistor, a lamp and a diode and explain the shapes?

1172.desc: Explain that a loudspeaker uses the motor effect to vibrate a cone with a varying current, and that a moving-coil microphone uses induction to turn sound vibrations into a varying current
1172.ev: Explains how a varying current moves a speaker cone
1172.q: If {{name}} connects a loudspeaker to an amplifier, can they explain how the electrical signal becomes sound?

997.desc: Map and draw the magnetic field patterns produced by a current in a straight wire (concentric circles) and in a solenoid (like a bar magnet), use the right-hand grip rule to find field direction, and plan an investigation showing that reversing the current reverses the field
997.ev: Describes the field pattern around a straight wire
997.q: If {{name}} places a compass next to a wire and switches on the current, can they explain why the needle moves?

1173.desc: Calculate magnification as image height ÷ object height (a ratio with no units), and relate it to the ray diagram
1173.q: If {{name}} measures a 2 cm object producing a 7 cm image, can they find the magnification and explain what it means?

1174.desc: Explain that objects have natural frequencies and that driving them at that frequency produces large-amplitude oscillations (resonance), with examples such as instruments, glasses and bridges
1174.q: If {{name}} sees a singer break a glass with a note, can they explain why only one particular pitch works?

1175.desc: Analyse data from experiments (e.g. trolleys pulled by different forces) to show that acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass
1175.ev: Plots acceleration against force and identifies a straight line through the origin
1175.q: If {{name}} is given a table of forces and accelerations for a trolley, can they plot a graph and explain what it shows about Newton's second law?

1176.desc: Evaluate the advantages of digital information (reliable storage, easy copying and sharing, compression) against drawbacks such as easy deletion, security risks and theft
1176.q: If {{name}} is deciding whether to keep only digital copies of family photos, can they weigh up the advantages and risks?

1177.desc: Apply conservation of momentum to explosions and recoil, where total momentum before is zero, to explain rockets, recoiling guns and jumping off a boat
1177.ev: Explains why total momentum after an explosion is zero
1177.q: If {{name}} jumps forward off a small rowing boat, can they explain why the boat moves backwards and estimate how fast?

1170.desc: Explain resistance in metals as electrons colliding with vibrating metal ions, and use this to explain why resistance rises with temperature and why current heats a wire
1170.ev: Describes electrons colliding with lattice ions
1170.q: If {{name}} sees a bulb filament's resistance increase as it glows, can they explain why using particles?

1178.desc: Explain why adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance (more paths), show the total is less than the smallest resistor, and calculate it with 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
1178.ev: Explains why adding a branch increases total current
1178.q: If {{name}} adds a second lamp in parallel, can they explain why the battery now supplies more current?

1179.desc: Describe how an analog signal is digitised by sampling at regular intervals and storing each sample as a binary number, and calculate how sample rate and bits per sample affect quality and file size
1179.ev: Digitises a simple waveform at a given sample rate
1179.q: If {{name}} records 10 s of audio at 44 100 samples per second with 16 bits each, can they estimate the file size?

1180.desc: Combine Ohm's law with series and parallel rules to find unknown currents, potential differences and resistances in mixed circuits
1180.ev: Finds every current and pd in a circuit with a parallel pair in series with a resistor
1180.q: If {{name}} is given a mixed circuit and the battery voltage, can they find the current through each resistor?

1181.desc: Explain that when waves meet their displacements add (superposition), producing constructive and destructive interference, and that the waves pass through each other unchanged
1181.ev: Adds two wave pulses on a diagram
1181.q: If {{name}} walks between two speakers playing the same note, can they explain why the sound gets louder and quieter in different places?

745.desc: Explain how drag increases with speed until it balances weight so a falling object reaches terminal velocity, and interpret velocity–time graphs for a skydiver
745.ev: Describes forces on a skydiver at each stage
745.q: If {{name}} sees a skydiver's speed graph level off, can they explain what is happening to the forces?

1182.desc: Describe the eye and the camera as converging-lens systems that form real images, and explain how short and long sight are corrected with diverging and converging lenses
1182.ev: Labels the parts of the eye that focus light
1182.q: If {{name}} is told a friend can't read distant signs, can they explain what is going wrong in the eye and which lens fixes it?

1147.desc: Explain total internal reflection when light in a denser medium meets a boundary at more than the critical angle, and apply it to optical fibres and endoscopes
1147.ev: States both conditions for total internal reflection
1147.q: If {{name}} sees light trapped inside a curved glass fibre, can they explain why it doesn't escape through the sides?

1183.desc: Use Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and, for an ideal transformer, Vp × Ip = Vs × Is to calculate voltages, currents and numbers of turns
1183.ev: Calculates secondary voltage from turns ratio
1183.q: If {{name}} needs 12 V from 230 V mains, can they work out a suitable turns ratio?

1185.desc: Explain how pulses of ultrasound are partly reflected at each boundary between materials, and how timing the echoes builds an image in prenatal scans, finds cracks in metal (non-destructive testing) and maps the sea bed
1185.ev: Explains why ultrasound is partly reflected at each tissue boundary
1185.q: If {{name}} sees an ultrasound scan of a baby, can they explain how echoes from different tissues make the picture?

1186.desc: Explain how grid operators meet changing demand through the day and year, the challenge of variable renewables, and the role of storage such as pumped hydro and batteries
1186.q: If {{name}} sees demand spike at half-time in a big match, can they explain how the grid keeps up?

1187.desc: Create a computational model (equations or a spreadsheet) that calculates the change in energy of one part of a system when the changes in the other parts and the flows in and out are known, and explain what each expression represents
1187.ev: Writes an energy balance equation for a system of two or three parts
1187.q: If {{name}} models a roller coaster car with friction, can they set up a calculation that tracks kinetic, potential and dissipated energy at each point?

1188.desc: Use energy conservation (energy lost by the hot object = energy gained by the cold object) with Q = mcΔT to calculate the final temperature of a mixture or an unknown specific heat capacity
1188.ev: Sets up the equation energy lost = energy gained
1188.q: If {{name}} mixes 200 g of water at 80 °C with 200 g of water at 20 °C, can they predict the final temperature and set up an equation that would work for unequal amounts?

1189.desc: Compare power lost in transmission cables at different voltages using P = I²R and P = IV, showing quantitatively why high-voltage transmission cuts losses
1189.ev: Calculates current in cables for a given power at two voltages
1189.q: If {{name}} compares sending 10 MW at 25 kV and at 400 kV, can they calculate how much less power is wasted?

747.desc: Describe and graph the exponential decay of charge, current and pd as a capacitor discharges through a resistor, and interpret the time constant RC
747.ev: Sketches charge against time during discharge
747.q: If {{name}} sees the voltage across a discharging capacitor halve every few seconds, can they explain why the graph has that shape?

1190.desc: Explain that a capacitor stores energy by separating equal and opposite charges on two plates (the charge Q on each plate), use Q = CV, and describe uses such as camera flashes and smoothing
1190.ev: Calculates charge stored for a given capacitance and pd
1190.q: If {{name}} sees a camera flash charge then fire, can they explain what the capacitor is doing?

1192.desc: Explain that an object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating towards the centre because its velocity direction changes, requiring a centripetal force supplied by tension, friction or gravity
1192.ev: Explains why constant speed in a circle still means acceleration
1192.q: If {{name}} whirls a ball on a string and the string snaps, can they predict which way the ball flies and explain why?

1193.desc: Use Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² to describe and predict the electrostatic force between two charged objects, comparing its form with gravitation
1193.ev: Calculates the force between two charges
1193.q: If {{name}} halves the distance between two charged balloons, can they predict how the force between them changes?

1194.desc: Explain that an induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it, and use this to predict poles and current directions
1194.ev: Predicts the pole formed when a magnet approaches a coil
1194.q: If {{name}} pushes a magnet's north pole into a coil, can they predict which pole forms at that end of the coil and explain why?

1195.desc: Distinguish elastic collisions (kinetic energy conserved) from inelastic ones (kinetic energy transferred to other stores), noting that momentum is conserved in both
1195.ev: Checks whether kinetic energy is conserved in a collision
1195.q: If {{name}} works out the kinetic energy before and after two trolleys stick together, can they explain why it went down even though momentum stayed the same?

1196.desc: Define electric field strength as force per unit charge, calculate it with E = F/Q, and for parallel plates use E = V/d to describe a uniform field
1196.ev: Calculates the force on a charge in a known field
1196.q: If {{name}} has two plates 2 cm apart with 400 V across them, can they calculate the field strength and the force on an electron?

1197.desc: Distinguish emf from terminal pd, explain internal resistance as energy lost inside the source, and use ε = I(R + r) to analyse cells
1197.ev: Explains why terminal pd drops when more current is drawn
1197.q: If {{name}} notices car headlights dim when the engine starts, can they explain why using internal resistance?

1198.desc: Explain that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, that hotter objects emit more and at shorter wavelengths, and that an object's temperature stays constant when it absorbs and emits at the same rate, applying this to Earth's temperature
1198.ev: Explains why a heated metal glows red then white
1198.q: If {{name}} watches a stove ring heating up, can they explain why its colour changes and what happens when its temperature stops rising?

1200.desc: Evaluate claims in media about health effects of EM radiation (mobile phones, Wi-Fi, sunbeds, X-rays), checking frequency, energy, dose, sources and evidence quality
1200.ev: Identifies the frequency band a claim is about
1200.q: If {{name}} reads a post claiming Wi-Fi causes cancer, can they judge the claim using what they know about frequency and evidence?

1201.desc: State that the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage, and use it to explain why faster motion, stronger fields and more turns give larger emfs
1201.ev: Explains induced emf in terms of rate of change
1201.q: If {{name}} spins a generator twice as fast, can they explain using Faraday's law what happens to the output voltage?

1202.desc: Resolve weight into components parallel and perpendicular to an inclined plane, and calculate the acceleration of an object sliding down a slope with or without friction
1202.ev: Resolves weight on a slope into two components
1202.q: If {{name}} is told a box sits on a 30° ramp, can they work out the part of its weight pulling it down the slope?

1203.desc: Explain that thermal energy spontaneously spreads from hotter to colder regions and becomes more evenly distributed (the second law of thermodynamics), and why this limits the efficiency of engines and power stations
1203.ev: States that heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never spontaneously the reverse
1203.q: If {{name}} is asked why an ice cube in a warm room never gets colder on its own, can they explain the rule about which way heat flows?

1205.desc: Explain that the intensity of light or sound from a point source falls with the inverse square of distance because the energy spreads over a larger area
1205.ev: Explains why doubling distance quarters intensity
1205.q: If {{name}} moves twice as far from a lamp, can they predict how bright it will appear and explain why?

1206.desc: Apply conservation of charge at junctions (currents in = currents out) and conservation of energy round any loop (sum of emfs = sum of pds) to analyse circuits
1206.ev: Uses the junction rule to find an unknown current
1206.q: If {{name}} knows the currents in two branches leaving a junction, can they find the current entering it and say which law they used?

468.desc: Use Newton's law of universal gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r² to describe and predict the gravitational force between two objects, including the inverse-square effect of distance
468.ev: Calculates the gravitational force between two masses
468.q: If {{name}} is told a satellite moves to twice its distance from Earth's centre, can they predict how the gravitational force changes?

940.desc: Calculate photon energy with E = hf and E = hc/λ, and use it to explain why higher-frequency radiation is more damaging
940.ev: Calculates the energy of a photon of given frequency
940.q: If {{name}} compares a UV photon and an infrared photon, can they calculate which carries more energy and by how much?

1008.desc: Explain that transverse waves can be polarised to oscillate in one plane, that longitudinal waves cannot, and use this as evidence that light is transverse; describe uses such as polarising sunglasses
1008.ev: Explains why only transverse waves can be polarised
1008.q: If {{name}} looks through two polarising filters and rotates one, can they explain why the view goes dark?

1209.desc: Explain how two resistors in series divide the supply pd in the ratio of their resistances, calculate output voltages, and use an LDR or thermistor to make a sensing circuit
1209.ev: Calculates the output pd of a potential divider
1209.q: If {{name}} builds a potential divider with a thermistor, can they predict whether the output rises or falls when it gets warmer?

1210.desc: Explain that oscillating charges in an aerial (driven by an alternating current) emit radio waves, and that absorbed radio waves induce an alternating current of the same frequency in a receiving aerial
1210.ev: Explains how an alternating current produces radio waves
1210.q: If {{name}} is asked how a radio picks up a station, can they explain what the radio wave does to electrons in the aerial?

194.desc: Analyse projectile motion by treating horizontal motion (constant velocity) and vertical motion (constant acceleration g) independently, and calculate range, time of flight and maximum height
194.ev: Explains why horizontal and vertical motion are independent
194.q: If {{name}} rolls a ball off a 1.25 m high table at 2 m/s, can they work out how far from the table it lands?

1212.desc: Explain that light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths, that more distant galaxies show greater red-shift, and how this supports the Big Bang model
1212.ev: Explains what red-shift means for spectral lines
1212.q: If {{name}} sees that a galaxy's spectral lines are shifted towards red, can they explain what it tells us about the galaxy's motion?

1213.desc: Use refractive index n = c/v and Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ to calculate angles of refraction and speeds of light in materials
1213.ev: Calculates the speed of light in glass from its refractive index
1213.q: If {{name}} measures a ray entering glass at 40° and leaving the surface at 25°, can they calculate the refractive index?

1214.desc: Use R = ρL/A to calculate resistance from resistivity, length and cross-sectional area, and compare materials
1214.ev: Calculates resistance of a wire of given dimensions
1214.q: If {{name}} has a copper wire 2 m long with a cross-section of 1 mm², can they calculate its resistance from the resistivity of copper?

1215.desc: Explain how solar cells release electrons when they absorb light of high enough frequency, producing a pd, and evaluate solar power output and limitations
1215.ev: Describes the energy transfer in a solar cell
1215.q: If {{name}} sees a solar-powered calculator stop working in dim light, can they explain why?

1216.desc: Interpret the decibel scale as logarithmic — each increase of 10 dB is ten times the intensity — and use it to judge risks of hearing damage
1216.ev: Explains why 80 dB is 100 times the intensity of 60 dB
1216.q: If {{name}} is told a concert is 110 dB and a busy street is 80 dB, can they say how many times more intense the concert is?

1217.desc: Explain standing waves on a string or in a pipe as the superposition of two waves travelling in opposite directions, identify nodes and antinodes, and relate harmonics to the notes of instruments
1217.ev: Labels nodes and antinodes on a standing wave
1217.q: If {{name}} presses a guitar string halfway along, can they explain why the note goes up an octave?

1211.desc: Explain that a moving source produces waves bunched up ahead (higher frequency) and stretched out behind (lower frequency), with examples from sirens and astronomy
1211.ev: Draws wavefronts from a moving source
1211.q: If {{name}} hears an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes, can they explain with a wavefront drawing what's happening?

1218.desc: Use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (real-is-positive convention) to find image distances, and calculate lens power in dioptres (P = 1/f, with f in metres)
1218.ev: Finds the image distance for a given focal length and object distance
1218.q: If {{name}} has a lens of focal length 10 cm and an object 15 cm away, can they calculate where the image forms?

767.desc: Use the principle that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, and apply it to braking distances and accelerating vehicles
767.q: If {{name}} is told a car's speed doubles, can they use energy and work ideas to explain why its braking distance becomes about four times longer?

1208.desc: Evaluate evidence that light behaves as a wave (diffraction, interference) and as particles called photons (photoelectric effect), and explain why scientists use whichever model fits a situation
1208.ev: Gives evidence for the wave model
1208.q: If {{name}} learns that, for some metals, dim blue light can knock electrons out but very bright red light can't, can they explain why this supports a particle model?
